verdicts.topic: Whether the grid reaches GitHub
verdicts.quote_a: code ships by commit through `git archive | ssh tar` because the grid can no longer fetch the private repository
verdicts.quote_b: Your Beethoven session already reaches GitHub: it cloned your two public repositories from the compute node. What it lacks is a login, so it cannot read the private
verdicts.explanation: The connect page (2026-10-14) agrees with the handoff that the grid cannot read the private repository. It adds the reason: the network reaches GitHub, but there is no login. Public clones working is consistent with that.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the connect page's statement: compute nodes reach GitHub, and private repositories need a token stored for git.

verdicts.topic: The login node rule
verdicts.quote_a: Nothing runs on the login node: every computation, render, plot and download is a job, even a one-minute one.
verdicts.quote_b: Never run anything that uses more than one CPU core for more than 60 seconds, loads a GPU, or exceeds 4 GB of memory on a login node.
verdicts.explanation: The onboarding (2026-10-13), in line with the lab recipe, forbids any computation on the login node, even a one-minute one. The playbook (2026-10-03) allows work under a ceiling of one core for 60 seconds and 4 GB, written as a general cluster template. Under the playbook a short single-core job would be allowed; under the onboarding it would not.
verdicts.resolution_hint: For the Wayne State grid, carry the lab's stricter rule from the onboarding and lab recipe, and mark the playbook's ceiling as a generic template.

verdicts.topic: Polling squeue
verdicts.quote_a: No `squeue` loop beyond about ten minutes
verdicts.quote_b: check at most once a minute and never in a tight loop
verdicts.explanation: The lab recipe limits how long an agent may poll in total. The playbook limits how often it may poll. Both rules can be followed together.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry both: poll at most once a minute, and for no more than about ten minutes before checkpointing and stopping.

verdicts.topic: Which workflow engine the pipeline uses
verdicts.quote_a: The head job is one `sbatch` on `reqp --qos=requeue --requeue --open-mode=append`, 2–4 CPUs, days of wall time.
verdicts.quote_b: A workflow engine cannot run on the login node, so Metaflow's scheduler would itself have to run inside a job.
verdicts.explanation: The lab recipe already runs the Nextflow head as a Slurm job, and the reforms checklist requires a workflow engine's scheduler to run inside a job. Both pages agree that an engine runs inside a job; they differ only on which engine an imaging pipeline would use, which the reforms page leaves open.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry: no imaging repository runs a workflow engine (lab recipe), and any engine's scheduler runs inside a job.

verdicts.topic: Account rules: pooling tokens against the token pool and a second account
verdicts.quote_a: Keep it one account. Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit
verdicts.quote_b: In the cloud, workers.yml runs workers in GitHub Actions on the token pool, and the Runs tab can cancel them.
verdicts.explanation: The playbook (2026-10-03) tells the reader to keep to one account and calls rotating accounts to widen the window a breach of the terms. The review (2026-10-21) describes cloud workers on a token pool. It also proposes picking a grid account 'the way pool.py picks a cloud slot', which spreads work across several of the owner's accounts. These pages do not reconcile the two positions.
verdicts.resolution_hint: The textbook should carry the playbook's rule and the later pool design side by side. The owner's recorded decision on coordinating his own several accounts settles which one holds.

verdicts.topic: hpcworker framework and Beethoven extension versions
verdicts.quote_a: hpcworker framework 11, extension 12.0.0
verdicts.quote_b: Since framework 22 the grid runs several named workers at once, each one a Remote Control environment.
verdicts.explanation: On 2026-10-03 the reforms checklist gives hpcworker framework 11 and extension 12.0.0. On 2026-10-21 the grid-workers page gives framework 22 to 23 and Beethoven 23.x.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry framework 22 to 23 and Beethoven 23.x as of 2026-10-21.

verdicts.topic: What the 24-hour release reads: commit date or push time
verdicts.quote_a: Idleness is read from the commit date, which whoever pushes sets, so a worker can keep a claim alive or let one lapse early by its clock (F8, open).
verdicts.quote_b: the board releases a claim whose branch has had no push for 24 hours
verdicts.explanation: The brief (2026-10-14) says idleness is read from the commit date and that F8, judging idleness by GitHub's push time, is still open. The review (2026-10-21) speaks of 24 hours with no push, but never says F8 landed. Its wording may be loose rather than a report of the fix.
verdicts.resolution_hint: This is settled by the record of F8's merge and release in symphony-protocol, or by the Release section of the protocol text after 2026-10-14.

verdicts.topic: Where the archived files are and whether they exist yet
verdicts.quote_a: regulatory folders are not in the repository since 2026-10-13: they live on the grid under
verdicts.quote_b: until he has, those links point at nothing and the files are read from git history
verdicts.explanation: The onboarding (2026-10-13) says the archived folders live on the grid under the shared archive, and that the link opens in a Beethoven session. A day later the connect page says the owner has yet to fill the archive with a script, and that until then the links point at nothing. The two disagree on whether the archive was filled.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the connect page's statement (2026-10-14): the links point at the shared archive, which is empty until the owner's script fills it, and git history serves meanwhile.

verdicts.topic: Who can read the holding on CephFS
verdicts.quote_a: the CephFS group has two members; the PI's home is not group-readable
verdicts.quote_b: Every approved student reads the whole holding except the two sets held under an agreement.
verdicts.explanation: The lab recipe (2026-09-27) lists as an open gap that students had no readable data path, to be closed by a group-readable export or an ACL. The holding manifest (2026-10-08) reports that route built: a named entry on the volume root for each approved AccessID, with folders opened as batches cut over. It also says the group still holds two people.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the holding manifest's access model of 2026-10-08: approved students read everything except VinDr-SpineXR and BUU-LSPINE.

verdicts.topic: Where the grid's GitHub credential is stored

verdicts.quote_b: git config --global credential.helper "store --file ~/.beethoven/git-credentials"
verdicts.explanation: The onboarding (2026-10-13) has issue 19's read token saved to a token file. The connect page (2026-10-14) stores a token in a git credential file read by git's store helper, and says issue 19 records exactly what that setup measures. The later page replaces the earlier procedure for the grid's GitHub login.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the connect page's procedure: the token in the git-credentials file under the private Beethoven folder, mode 600, read by git's credential helper.

verdicts.topic: How a Claude project is set up for this programme

verdicts.resolution_hint: Cite the rule once, from the playbook's compliance section.

verdicts.topic: The comparator cannot be exceeded at any reachable n

verdicts.topic: No published work uses DRRs to supply level identity to a 2-D model

verdicts.topic: Published class-agnostic C-arm detection and Rao's 0.964

canonical_check.relation: superseded-by (omitted by the clustering, which gives superseded: [])
canonical_check.why: The board's own related_titles say it is superseded by Spine Program Decisions, and the records bear it out: the decisions page repeats the board's SOTA, commercial-clean, 39/39 and replacement-rule sentences verbatim and closes the board's open IRB item; the clustering lists neither a supersession nor a duplicate.

canonical_check.relation: duplicate-text of (omitted by the clustering, which gives duplicates: [])
canonical_check.why: Four sentences are shared nearly word for word; the records support a duplicate relation the clustering does not list.

The onboarding is canonical in the clustering, but the next day's connect note contradicts it on the archive (points at nothing), the credential file name and the grid's reach to GitHub; it is canonical only for the programme rules, not for the grid steps.

The recipe is the one statement of the chain rules (PREREG sha256, afterany, no squeue loops, private-forever list) and nothing later contradicts those; its access and v10-mirror lines are dated and stale.

The handoff is the fullest numbered record and names the catalog as the rule; the directions note of the same date is its companion, and the two disagree only on the transitional counts (0 against 33 in hand).

The directions note's order of work (no training before gates G0 to G3) is overtaken by the grid pipeline's version 1 by 28 October; both are canonical in the clustering, but on the order of work the later one governs and should be marked as superseding the earlier on that point.
The pipeline is the newest plan and the only one with dates; its registry tally (111) does not match the registry page of the day before (60), so it is canonical for the schedule, not for the counts.

clusters.unsourced_summary: The cluster asserts, with no source in any record, the comparator claim that 97.6% cannot be exceeded at any reachable n (the handoff and the literature note, which also attributes the figure to LevelCheck while the directions note attributes it to Manbachi 2018 assisted reads); the novelty claims that no published work uses DRRs to supply level identity to a 2-D model (decisions) and that the best registration-free naming is 73.3% and class-agnostic C-arm detection reaches 0.96 to 0.98 (counting-from-the-sacrum), beside the literature note's own doubt that Rao's 0.964 may be cadaver and phantom only; the handoff's statements that every planning value assumed 95 to 99% that no measurement supports, that the grid can no longer fetch the private repository, and that nothing after 2026-09-27 changed the banks or models as far as any file shows, where the lab recipe says 0 of 79 manifest keys carry a job id, so no file could show it; the holding page's claim that every source is a public release or was synthesised from one, while the registry holds VinDr and two other sets under agreements and DysphagiaBank by registration; the duplicated board and decisions sentences (published SOTA AUC 0.84 at 62.3% prevalence, the commercial-clean list, 39/39 lean back, three replacement rules none beat the one that ships), none of which names a paper, a run or a catalog key; the onboarding and connect notes' statement that the framework empties hpcworker's folders; the playbook's premise that most compute nodes cannot reach the internet, which the connect note contradicts for this grid, and its and the checklist's reading of the terms as one person, one account, restated beside a token-pool design; and the grid-worker plan's premises that the laptop cannot keep several desktops signed in, that framework 22 keeps each worker to its own account with a stable environment id, and the review's that a successor job continues the same Remote Control session for up to seven days, all marked unmeasured by their own records.
clusters.stale_summary: Dated or pending as of the records: the handoff (2026-10-08) carries the Beethoven store listing in progress, the Ceph migration in progress, the provisional filing not recorded after the 2026-09-25 disclosure, 14 dataset requests drafted and none sent, and CNS 31 Oct to 4 Nov; the directions note (2026-10-08) says nothing ran on the grid, the public CTSpinoPelvic1K mirror is v10 with id 29 (the lab recipe said the same on 2026-09-27), and 33 graded against 71 to 142 expected; the lab recipe's two-member CephFS group and the 0 of 79 job-id keys are as of 2026-09-27; the onboarding (2026-10-13) leaves issue 19 open on whether the grid reaches GitHub and sends students to an archive the connect note (2026-10-14) says is not filled yet; the reforms checklist (2026-10-03) names framework 11 and extension 12.0.0 and says none of its gates exists yet, while the 2026-10-21 plan and review name framework 22 and Beethoven 23.x with no second worker started and only the Wayne State account signed in; the brief (2026-10-14) says nothing after 0.4.1 is released and F8 is open; the registry (2026-10-20) marks VinDr's determination pending, requests 1 to 14 never sent, no bank built for the geometry solved 2026-09-23, and sample counts empty until a grid job runs; the grid pipeline (2026-10-21) has gate words under review in PR #54, no job run, 5 of 20 recipes ready, 22 registry entries with no shard, 26 requested and 5 granted in spine-datasets, CT-RATE off by the owner's decision of 21 October, the RSNA RATIC link expiring 2026-10-28 02:38 UTC, one press remaining for the owner, and a schedule of 25 October (frames drawn), 28 October (version 1 trained), 30 October (provisional filed) and 2 November (CNS mini-oral 66629); the any-view plan (2026-10-21) has the census job built in PR #76 and not yet run; the AIDAS proposal's deadline of 16 October 2026 has passed with no record of submission; and the September pages (counting-from-the-sacrum, the board) describe a training run and an audit as running, and the IRB files as public, both overtaken by the decisions page.
clusters.notes: All 19 records were read in full; the plain texts were searched once for the duplicated board/decisions sentences, the afterany rule, DysphagiaBank and the 4.3-point figure, and the extraction's line breaks and characters made every pattern but one miss, so verbatim duplicate findings rest on the records' quote fields rather than on the texts. Two facts loaded into this session from the repositories' own memory, not from the records, bear on candidates and are left out of them: SchwingNet's memory says WSU IRB HPR 2026-330 of 29 September 2026 covers VinDr-SpineXR under its PhysioNet agreement, which would make the registry's 'determination pending' line stale; and the fetch-chain memory says each fetch refuses to exceed the volume's free space minus 1 TB where the grid pipeline artifact says minus 5 TB. The repository's PROTOCOL.md now dates idleness by the push GitHub received, which resolves the F8 candidate in the review's favour; that too is outside the records. People are named by role throughout; the owner's first name appears inside quoted text where the record carried it. No e-mail address, phone number or home address appears in any record quoted. The cluster is confidential patent material by the any-view plan's and the project goal's own words.

clusters.cluster: Symphony: the protocol, its evidence and its place

candidates.topic: Whether Symphony has any hosted piece of its own (the 'no server' claim)
candidates.statement_a: Symphony has nothing to host: no server, database or daemon of the project's own (2026-10-15).
candidates.quote_a: There is nothing to host. No server, database or daemon of the project's own
candidates.statement_b: The product has a webhook server (symphony-app, undeployed, to be deleted) and an approved but unbuilt Cloudflare sign-in service for the control panel (2026-10-13).
candidates.quote_b: Hosted pieces: nothing of ours runs. The webhook server is not deployed, and the Cloudflare sign-in service is approved but not built
candidates.why_it_matters: 'No server' holds for the claim protocol only; a planner who reads the spec alone would not budget, secure or review the stateless sign-in service the control panel depends on, nor know the webhook stage still exists in symphony-app's code until its deletion lands.

candidates.topic: Whether coordination in Actions with no server distinguishes Symphony
candidates.statement_a: The headline design claim is a serverless protocol in which git lets exactly one of two racing creations win.
candidates.quote_a: with no server of its own... git lets exactly one of two racing creations win
candidates.statement_b: The spec's own list of what not to claim says serverless coordination in Actions is shared by unsorry and gh-aw.
candidates.quote_b: Coordination that runs in Actions with no server: unsorry and gh-aw do it too.
candidates.why_it_matters: A grant or comparison that leads with 'serverless' as the distinction over-claims; only the combination of five mechanisms is claimed unique (competitors l.98 and manual l.243 agree with the spec, the opening sentence does not).

candidates.topic: Whether a subscription setup-token is sanctioned for shared CI use
candidates.statement_a: The setup-token is a one-year credential sanctioned for CI from the cheapest paid plan up (2026-10-09).
candidates.quote_a: Claude Pro's setup-token (a one-year OAuth credential, sanctioned for CI from the cheapest paid plan up) powers both @claude mentions and the scheduled worker
candidates.statement_b: Anthropic documents the token but advises an API key for a secret shared across repositories, and whether several workers on one plan are ordinary individual usage is open (R6).
candidates.quote_b: Anthropic advises an API key for a secret shared across repositories and says plan limits 'assume ordinary, individual usage'
candidates.why_it_matters: The ladder's bottom rung prices the whole machine on one Pro token in CI; the spec and the competitors note grade that usage Open, so the $17 rung may not be an approved configuration for an organization secret shared by workers.

candidates.topic: Pooling several accounts' tokens to widen the usage window
candidates.statement_a: Pooling several users' tokens or rotating accounts is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; more window means an API key.
candidates.quote_a: Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; if the workload needs more than one subscription's window, it is a workload for an API key.
candidates.statement_b: The owner's accounts form one pool of organization secrets picked by code, then CooperBench runs on it (decision of 2026-10-13, 'knowing the terms question').
candidates.quote_b: one organization secret per account, SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_<NAME>... SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner reading the playbook would refuse the pool; one reading the handoff would build it (and the repository's memory index of 2026-10-22 says the token pool is built). The handoff limits it to the owner's own accounts and asks that the Usage Policy be re-read before 2026-11-12; the playbook makes no such allowance.

candidates.topic: GITHUB_TOKEN's hourly request limit that binds the board and benchmark
candidates.statement_a: 1,000 requests an hour per repository, with no retry on 429 (risk 5).
candidates.quote_a: GITHUB_TOKEN gets 1,000 requests an hour per repository and the library has no retry on 429
candidates.statement_b: 1,000 an hour, but 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud, and the organization is inferred to be on Enterprise Cloud.
candidates.quote_b: GITHUB_TOKEN is limited to 1,000 API requests an hour per repository, 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud
candidates.why_it_matters: The spec, manual and competitors note say the 1,000 limit probably binds before minutes (R3); if the organization is Enterprise Cloud as the handoff infers (l.47, l.1566), the binding limit is 15x higher and the scale ceiling they warn of is wrong for this organization, though right for an adopter on Free.

candidates.topic: Which GitHub plan the project itself runs on
candidates.statement_a: The bottom rung is a personal account: $17 a month for Claude, $0 guaranteed GitHub bill, GitHub Pro at $4 if private.
candidates.quote_a: $17 a month runs the whole machine... $0 is the guaranteed GitHub bill... 3,000... on both the $4 GitHub Pro plan and the GitHub Team plan
candidates.statement_b: sdlc-template is internal, so the enterprise is an Enterprise Cloud account; Code Security was not bought as of 2026-10-08.
candidates.quote_b: sdlc-template is internal (Symphony constraint) and internal visibility belongs to organizations owned by an enterprise account, so the enterprise OpenGrid is an Enterprise Cloud account; GitHub Code Security was not bought as of 2026-10-08
candidates.why_it_matters: The ladder's per-feature prices describe an adopter, not the owner's organization; a planner costing the owner's own runs (50,000 included minutes, 15,000 token requests, merge queue on private repositories) would read the wrong rung.

candidates.topic: Billed minutes saved by the board's six-hourly cron fallback
candidates.statement_a: Cutting the board's cron from hourly to six-hourly saves about 630 billed minutes a month (750 to 120).
candidates.quote_a: the board's cron fallback cut from hourly to six-hourly, saving a private repository about 630 billed minutes a month
candidates.statement_b: Schedules ran hours late and dropped most slots: the hourly board cron ran 16 of about 87 slots, the ten-minute sweep 8 of about 300.
candidates.quote_b: Schedules are best effort. Measured here, they ran hours late and dropped most slots. Every cron in the design is affected
candidates.why_it_matters: The ladder's savings are computed on slots that never ran; and the handoff's measurement means the six-hourly fallback cannot be relied on to release idle claims or refresh the board on time, which the protocol's Release section assumes.

candidates.topic: Status of the F8 fix (idle clock read from GitHub's push record, symphony-protocol#35)
candidates.statement_a: The F8 fix is written but not merged (2026-10-15).
candidates.quote_a: A fix that reads GitHub's own record of the push is written but not merged (finding F8)
candidates.statement_b: #35 merged on main on 2026-10-15, unreleased, with one gap (a claim's first push).
candidates.quote_b: by the head's committer date in 0.4.1 and in every copy today, by GitHub's record of the push on main since #35 of 2026-10-15, unreleased
candidates.why_it_matters: The spec (risk 13: 'The unmerged F8 fix') and manual were written the same day #35 merged; a planner reading them would count F8 open and the defect count at 'one waits on the owner', while the competitors note counts it merged (twelve fixes on main). Every adopted copy still reads the committer date until 0.5.0 is published.

candidates.topic: Whether the protocol's validation is exhaustive or bounded
candidates.statement_a: The shipped code is checked exhaustively through every interleaving of scripted workers.
candidates.quote_a: **The shipped protocol code is checked exhaustively.** A validation harness drives the shipped library through every interleaving of scripted workers
candidates.statement_b: It is bounded checking of small worlds, not a proof; the deeper searches are the unmerged deep lane.
candidates.quote_b: This is bounded checking of small worlds, not a proof. The deeper searches and the real-git world are the deep lane, symphony-protocol#21, still unmerged
candidates.why_it_matters: 'Exhaustively' invites the reading that the protocol is proved; the brief and the spec's own grades say the search is exhaustive only within a depth and a worker count, and the real-git and github.com behaviour (R4) is not covered.

candidates.topic: Number of defects the validation harness found
candidates.statement_a: Twelve defects, F1 to F12, six of them left (2026-10-13).
candidates.quote_a: the prototype found twelve defects, F1 to F12
candidates.statement_b: Nineteen defects: six fixed in 0.4.1, eleven on main, one settled in the spec, one (F8) open (2026-10-15).
candidates.quote_b: found 19 defects: six are fixed in release 0.4.1, eleven more on main ahead of the next release, one (F16) was settled by changing the spec, and one (F8, idleness read from the committer date) waits on the owner
candidates.why_it_matters: The handoff's work list (F7, F12, F4, F14, F9, F13, F2, F8, then the stuck claim) is the owner's ordered plan; a planner must know F13 to F19 were found after it and that 0.5.0's scope grew.

candidates.topic: Fixes on symphony-protocol's main after release 0.4.1
candidates.statement_a: Eleven fixes on main, not yet released (2026-10-15).
candidates.quote_a: found 19 defects: six are fixed in release 0.4.1, eleven on main but not yet released, one was settled in the spec, and one (F8) is open
candidates.statement_b: Twelve fixes on main and unreleased, a thirteenth (F16) settled in the spec (2026-10-16).
candidates.quote_b: 0.4.1 of 2026-10-13 is the last release, and twelve fixes made since are on main and unreleased (a thirteenth finding, F16, was settled in the spec), so an adopter waits for 0.5.0
candidates.why_it_matters: The twelfth is #35 (F8); the two counts differ by whether that merge is counted, so a release note or grant text must pick the later number.

candidates.topic: Number of mutants the harness catches
candidates.statement_a: 59 mutants, each caught (2026-10-14).
candidates.quote_a: 59 deliberately broken copies of the rules (mutants) are each caught
candidates.statement_b: 93 mutants caught, 109 on main after #35 (2026-10-16).
candidates.quote_b: 93 mutants... were each caught, 109 on main after #35
candidates.why_it_matters: Three figures (59, 93, 109) describe the same check two days apart; a document quoting the brief understates the evidence by half and none of the three is a released figure.

candidates.topic: Size of the interleaving search run against the oracle
candidates.statement_a: Two workers to depth 5, about 29,500 states; three workers to depth 4 (the required check's lane).
candidates.quote_a: two workers on one issue to depth 5 (about 29,500 states), three workers to depth 4... None found a violation
candidates.statement_b: 16.7 million states at depth 8 and 18.8 million with two issues at depth 7 (the weekly deep searches, run of record 2026-10-14).
candidates.quote_b: 16.7 million states at depth 8, and 18.8 million with two issues at depth 7
candidates.why_it_matters: The brief calls the deep lane (#21) unmerged while the spec reports its run of record from the same day; a planner must know which depth runs in CI on every pull request (5) and which only weekly or by hand (7 and 8, manual l.221).

candidates.topic: The brief's accounting of the seventeen guarantees at commit b5f098d
candidates.statement_a: At b5f098d (2026-10-14): 12 guarantees hold, 2 hold only if commit dates are honest, 1 known broken, 1 partly checked, 1 not checked.
candidates.quote_a: On symphony-protocol's main today (b5f098d, after F15 and F16 merged this evening), 12 hold, 2 hold only if commit dates are honest, 1 is known broken, 1 is partly checked and 1 is not checked.

candidates.quote_b: GitHub enforces the claim only at its creation, since claude/** stays out of every ruleset... the local push guard was found to judge a lease... by its own directory rather than the clone a git -C push names
candidates.why_it_matters: The brief's tally is the one most likely to be quoted ('12 of 17 hold'); it predates both the F8 merge and the guard's directory bug, so the numbers in each bucket moved within two days.

candidates.topic: Planned size of the coordbench benchmark of Symphony
candidates.statement_a: 42 pairs, 378 sessions, detecting only gaps of about 26 to 30 points (2026-10-13).
candidates.quote_a: 42 pairs give 80 percent power only for differences of about 26 to 30 points, 100 pairs about 18 to 20, 300 about 10 to 12, all 652 about 8
candidates.statement_b: 50 pairs from 20 tasks, five arms, Sonnet 5.5, 120 minutes per agent, one seed, detecting about 25 points (2026-10-14).
candidates.quote_b: 50 pairs from 20 tasks, five arms (sdlc, solo, coop, coop-git, team), Claude Sonnet 5.5 for every agent, 120 minutes per agent, one seed... At 50 pairs it can detect a gap of about 25 points
candidates.why_it_matters: Cost, calendar and the detectable effect all follow the pair count; three plans (42, 50, then 35 new plus redo) exist within three days.

candidates.topic: Planned size of the coordbench benchmark of Symphony (second move)
candidates.statement_a: 50 pairs from 20 tasks (2026-10-14).
candidates.quote_a: 50 pairs from 20 tasks, five arms (sdlc, solo, coop, coop-git, team)
candidates.statement_b: 35 new pairs under five arms plus the runs to redo, chosen 2026-10-15, against a roughly 15-point noise floor.
candidates.quote_b: The coordbench full run you chose on 2026-10-15 (35 new pairs under five arms, plus the runs to redo)... roughly 15-point noise floor
candidates.why_it_matters: The spec's R1 names a noise floor larger than the gap 35 pairs can detect; a planner must reconcile the pair count with the power table in the handoff before reporting any result.

candidates.quote_b: has run 8 pairs: Symphony's arm passed 6 of 8 like every two-agent arm, one agent 5 of 8, and no difference is significant (every exact McNemar p is 1.000...). It is a pilot, and its token and dollar figures are inflated by a prompt of about 78,000 to 82,000 tokens

candidates.quote_b: has run a pilot and a step of 8 pairs, and its harness audit found 11 of that step's 40 runs spoiled (a full disk, a pair spawned twice), so its figures are not reportable

verdicts.topic: Whether Symphony has any hosted piece of its own (the 'no server' claim)
verdicts.quote_a: No server, database or daemon of the project's own: the forge is the lock, the CI is the scheduler, and the repository is the state.

verdicts.explanation: The spec (2026-10-15) says Symphony's coordination has nothing to host. The handoff (2026-10-13) says the same thing, that nothing of the project's runs: the webhook server is not deployed and the sign-in service is not built. The two agree on what runs today. The handoff only adds two pieces that exist in code or in a plan.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the spec's 'nothing to host' for the coordination layer. Add the handoff's note that symphony-app's undeployed webhook stage (to be deleted) and the approved, unbuilt sign-in service for the control panel exist outside it.

verdicts.topic: Whether coordination in Actions with no server distinguishes Symphony
verdicts.quote_a: Symphony makes a GitHub repository the coordinator of Claude Code agents, with no server of its own.
verdicts.quote_b: Coordination that runs in Actions with no server: unsorry and gh-aw do it too.
verdicts.explanation: The competitors note (2026-10-16) opens with this as a description, not as one of its three 'better by design' claims. The same note says 'Not unique alone: unsorry and gh-aw are serverless in Actions too' and puts 'Coordination in Actions with no server' under What not to claim, word for word as the spec (2026-10-15) does. The two documents agree.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry serverless coordination as shared with unsorry and gh-aw (spec section 8). Present only the combination of mechanisms as the claim.

verdicts.topic: Whether a subscription setup-token is sanctioned for shared CI use
verdicts.quote_a: Claude Pro's `setup-token` (a one-year OAuth credential, sanctioned for CI from the cheapest paid plan up)
verdicts.quote_b: Anthropic advises an API key for a secret shared across repositories and says plan limits "assume ordinary, individual usage"
verdicts.explanation: The ladder (2026-10-09) calls the setup-token 'sanctioned for CI'. The competitors note (2026-10-16) cites Anthropic's GitHub Actions and legal pages. Those pages document the token but advise an API key for a shared secret and leave open whether several workers on one plan count as ordinary use. The note also lists 'Anthropic approves agents on a subscription in CI' under what not to claim. The ladder's wording overstates what the later, sourced reading supports.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the competitors note's wording (also spec 9.5): Anthropic documents the token for claude-code-action, advises an API key for a shared secret, and question R6 is open. Drop 'sanctioned'.

verdicts.topic: Pooling several accounts' tokens to widen the usage window
verdicts.quote_a: Keep it one account. Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; if the workload needs more than one subscription's window, it is a workload for an API key.
verdicts.quote_b: The owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator of the owner's, each worker on one account's token, knowing the terms question.
verdicts.explanation: The Slurm playbook (2026-10-03) calls rotating accounts to widen the usage window prohibited behaviour. The handoff (2026-10-13) designs a pool with one organization secret per account, SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_<NAME>, to spread runs over the owner's own accounts. It does this under an owner decision that names the terms question without settling it. The two pages disagree on whether this is allowed.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Record the pool as the owner's decision of 2026-10-13, taken knowing the terms question, not as compliant. Keep the playbook's statement as the opposing reading until Anthropic answers in writing (spec R6).

verdicts.topic: GITHUB_TOKEN's hourly request limit that binds the board and benchmark

verdicts.quote_b: GITHUB_TOKEN is limited to 1,000 API requests an hour per repository, 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud
verdicts.explanation: Both pages give 1,000 requests an hour per repository as the base limit. The handoff (2026-10-13) adds the Enterprise Cloud exception of 15,000. The spec (2026-10-15) states the general limit that applies to adopters on other plans. Read with their scopes, the two do not conflict.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 1,000 an hour per repository, with the handoff's 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud. Note that the project's own organization is inferred to be on Enterprise Cloud.

verdicts.topic: Which GitHub plan the project itself runs on

verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the ladder as adopter pricing. Carry the handoff's Enterprise Cloud reading, marked as inferred, as the project's own plan.

verdicts.topic: Billed minutes saved by the board's six-hourly cron fallback
verdicts.quote_a: the board's cron fallback cut from hourly to six-hourly, saving a private repository about 630 billed minutes a month
verdicts.quote_b: sdlc-template-test board.yml (cron '17 * * * *') 16 scheduled runs from 2026-10-09T09:11Z to 2026-10-13T00:42Z (~87 slots)
verdicts.explanation: The ladder (2026-10-09) prices the hourly fallback at about 750 minutes a month and the six-hourly one at about 120. That arithmetic assumes every cron slot runs. The handoff (2026-10-13) measured an hourly board cron that ran 16 of about 87 slots and a ten-minute sweep that ran 8 of about 300. It concludes that schedules 'ran hours late and dropped most slots'. The 630-minute saving therefore rests on a firing rate the measurement contradicts.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the handoff's measured run counts. Give the ladder's minute figures only as upper bounds that assume every slot fires; a month of billed minutes for the board workflow would settle the real cost.

They give conflicting sizes for the same manipulation.

canonical_check.why: The clustering lists no superseded or duplicate relation to bear out. The brief (2026-10-14) is the one artifact that tallies the seventeen guarantees and names which lane checks each; it is canonical for that, though its numbers (59 mutants, depth 5, F8 open, deep lane unmerged) are the oldest in the cluster and the spec and competitors note carry the later ones.

Dated 2026-10-16, it is the latest word on the validation numbers (twelve fixes on main, 109 mutants, #35 merged, the guard's directory bug) and the only one that withdraws the 8-pair coordbench figures; it overlaps the spec heavily on CooperBench and prior art and should be read for the 'what not to claim' list.

The spec is the source the manual, the competitors note and the brief cite by section; it alone grades each claim (Verified, Inferred, Reported, Open) and lists the risks and research questions. Its one weakness is that it reports the 8-pair pass counts that the competitors note later calls not reportable.

It is the reader's guide to the spec and adds the verification passes (verify/02's three findings, the adversarial search of 25 systems) that the spec summarises; it duplicates the spec's figures rather than superseding them, so it is canonical as the method record, not as a number source.

The handoff (2026-10-13) is the only record of the decisions of that night (the pool, the runtime, the QA gate, spine-program's state, the measured dropped cron slots, the plan ladder's unconfirmed $4 prices) and says itself its state lines were not rechecked against GitHub; it is canonical for decisions and dated state, not for numbers the later three artifacts moved. The ladder (2026-10-09), left non-canonical, is nonetheless the cluster's only pricing source with a verification date and should be read beside it.

clusters.unsourced_summary: The cluster asserts several load-bearing claims with no source opened. The taxonomy spec (SchwingNet/symphony-and-beethoven-taxonomy-spec-lcbqro) and the competitors note (symphony-template/symphony-versus-competitors-lynwzk) both carry Cursor's report that naive locks collapsed 20 agents to the throughput of two or three and a 2026 noise-floor study putting single-seed gains under about 15 points inside noise; both are graded Reported and unnamed, the competitors note says no primary source was opened for either, and the brief (symphony-template/symphony-in-brief-9cdciz) says its Cursor row is from memory because cursor.com is blocked. The spec's argument that GitHub's free public minutes are alone in the market rests on four withdrawal dates (Travis 2020, GitLab 2021, Azure DevOps 2026 and 2027, Cirrus 2026-06-01) of which it verifies two and the manual (symphony-template/symphony-and-beethoven-taxonomy-manual-re4jtx) still asks a pass to confirm, plus a CircleCI credit cap 'Reported, from its pricing page by search'. The spec appends 'Self-hosted runners are free on every plan' to a cited quote without a citation of its own, and its risk 3 (the account reached its weekly limit on 2026-10-15) and risk 9 (Wayne State's approval, no BAA on a personal plan, Remote Control under HIPAA) link no record. The atomic claim on github.com is stated as fact by the shared plan (symphony-template/shared-multi-account-claude-project-plan-rqzwh9), the build plan (symphony-template/sdlc-build-plan-bjzikn) and the brief while the spec's R4 leaves it open, the canary's C7 runs by hand and the manual's verify/02 ran on a scratch repository. 'Branch protection on a private repository needs a paid plan' is sourced to a docs page in the shared plan, marked 'to be checked, not assumed' in the build plan and attributed to 'document 25' in the primitives spec (symphony-template/sdlc-primitives-spec-ldx4zd), and no artifact records the check. The grid review (symphony-template/grid-and-cloud-claude-workers-review) and the handoff (symphony-template/symphony-handoff) use a 90-minute cloud-worker limit, a seven-day window for remote-control --continue and 'six 90-minute runs' per schedule without saying where they were read; the shared plan's 'hooks are not loaded in a Project with several repos' and its February 2026 ban reports (a blog's guess, unconfirmed by Anthropic) are likewise untested here. The ladder (symphony-template/the-dollar-per-feature-ladder-9ymg61) alone gives Windows 1.7x and macOS 10x runner multipliers and 'about a minute per pull request event', the figure its whole monthly-minute arithmetic rests on. The handoff could not confirm the GitHub Pro and Team $4 prices the ladder says it verified, and its 'enterprise OpenGrid' name has no source.
clusters.stale_summary: Everything in the cluster is dated 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-16 except the two grid notes read on 21 October, and much of it is 'as of' or 'not yet'. Release state: the brief (10-14), spec (10-15), manual (10-15) and competitors note (10-16) all say 0.4.1 of 2026-10-13 is the last release and an adopter waits for 0.5.0; the template's own memory index of 2026-10-22 says the template vendors 0.5.0, merged in the library and awaiting the owner's approval, so whether it is published must be re-read. The brief's guarantee tally is 'today (b5f098d)' and predates the F8 merge (#35, 2026-10-15) and the push guard's git -C directory bug found the same day; the spec and manual call the F8 fix unmerged on the day it merged. The deep lane symphony-protocol#21 is 'still unmerged' in the brief; the canary is 'not adopted yet' and C7 runs by hand. The brief's 'overlaps by file name only' and the spec's 'overlap detection by file' predate the symbol-level Locks and overlap check (switch at advise since 2026-10-20, per the template's PROTOCOL.md as loaded). The spec's and competitors' 'Not built: the qa check, the cap of 10 runs, the public runtime, the control panel, the account pool' is partly out of date: the memory index describes the control panel and the token pool as existing. The handoff (10-13) says its claims were not rechecked against GitHub; its pending list (Beethoven 20.0.0 to the store, beethoven-qa tags v4.0.0 and v5.0.0, the webhook stage to delete, the Cloudflare sign-in service approved but not built, the Actions box ticked by Symphony Setup) and its recommendation to keep the up-to-date-branch rule are superseded by the memory's 2026-10-20 rules (SymphonyBoard applies settings via settings.yml with Symphony Setup as fallback; the up-to-date rule off everywhere). The ladder (10-09) names the repository sdlc-template, prices verified 2026-10-09, a CLAUDE_WORKER switch and a 103-agent run, and computes savings on cron slots the handoff later measured as mostly dropped; Claude Enterprise's price 'could not be verified'. The shared plan's Linear queue, routine coordinator and hourly schedule were replaced on 2026-10-09. Beethoven versions move through the cluster: hpcworker framework 11 (REFORMS checklist) to 22-23 (grid notes, 21 Oct); extension 12.0.0 to 20.0.0 (handoff, spec) to 23.x (several-grid-workers); beethoven-qa v2.0.0 tagged 2026-10-07 (encapsulated) to v3.0.0 last tag with main at 5.0.0 (handoff), while the memory index expects 6.0.0 or later. 'None of the REFORMS gates exists' (checklist) became 'one module, splits.py' (spec) and SchwingNet's memory now describes a split check in CI; Metaflow is 'chosen, not built' in the spec and manual while SchwingNet's memory describes tools/flow.py submitting Slurm jobs. The coordbench picture is three days of moving state (one coop smoke pair, then 8 pairs with 6 of 8, then those 40 runs 'not reportable' with 11 spoiled), a chosen full run of 35 new pairs whose execution is not in the records, and the owner's hold on its numbers. The grid review says no second worker has started and the Wayne State Max account is the only one signed in (21 Oct); the onboarding (10-13) tells students to wait on issue 19 for whether the grid can reach GitHub, which a Beethoven session answered on 2026-10-14. Pending dates fall due soon after 2026-10-22: pull_request_target blocked by default on public repositories from 2026-11-02, Anthropic's Usage Policy clause on routing through consumer subscriptions on 2026-11-12 (the handoff asks that it be re-read before then), ubuntu-latest to 26.04 with Python 3.14.4 in November 2026, bare mode becoming claude -p's default (date unstated), Azure DevOps turning existing public projects private in 2027, and GitHub Code Security 'not bought as of 2026-10-08'.
clusters.notes: All seventeen records were read whole and the plain texts grepped for every quote; quotes are copied from the text files (a few long lines are cut at a clause boundary, and one brief line carrying a redaction marker inside a commit hash was avoided). Dates in 'why it matters' come from the records' own headers. Where a candidate says what the repository looks like on 2026-10-22, the source is the CLAUDE.md, PROTOCOL.md and memory index loaded into this session as project instructions (not the inventory records), and each such use is named as 'the memory index' or 'PROTOCOL.md as loaded'; nothing was filled from general memory. The clustering gave no superseded or duplicate relations, so the canonical_check records agreement with the five canonical ids and why, and suggests the ladder be read beside them as the only dated price source. The artifact symphony-template/claude-chat-vs-claude-code-architectural-analysis-snuzfd carries no Symphony claim (it compares the chat and Claude Code surfaces) and yielded no candidate; symphony-template/beethoven-build-roadmap-sttvvw and SchwingNet/reforms-compliance-checklist-bpzdoi are from 2026-10-03 and predate the protocol, so their candidates concern Beethoven's engine and gates only. The two grid notes (grid-and-cloud-claude-workers-review, several-grid-workers-one-per-project) were read on 21 October, after the cluster's stated 13-16 October window, and are the freshest state in the cluster. Three candidates have artifact_b equal to artifact_a (an internal inconsistency in the handoff's copy count, the shared plan's hooks claim, and the ladder's own run-time figure); the schema allows that for stale and unsourced kinds, and the handoff case is marked contradiction because the two statements sit in one document. People are named by role only (the owner, a student, a Claude Code team member).

clusters.cluster: Symphony's origins: cswap, the primitives and the two Claude surfaces

candidates.topic: The work queue: Linear or GitHub Issues
candidates.statement_a: The plan of 2026-10-08 makes Linear the queue, with states Todo, Claimed, In review and Done and a label per account; the claim branch is named after the Linear issue (claude/LIN-123).
candidates.quote_a: Linear holds the work queue and the conversation about each task.
candidates.statement_b: On 2026-10-09 the owner chose GitHub Issues as the queue and deferred Linear; every later artifact (the ladder, the brief, the taxonomy, the onboarding) has issues as the queue and claude/N as the branch.
candidates.quote_b: On 2026-10-09 [the owner] chose GitHub Issues and asked for the repository side first, as a GitHub template repository built from the bottom up with no export or import in its first layer (the sdlc-template work in the same thread); Linear and the materializer come later.
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner reading only the 2026-10-08 plan would set up a Linear team, a Claimed state and LIN-numbered branches; Symphony's claim lock, board and release all read GitHub issue numbers, and the Linear connector was never wired.

candidates.topic: Who releases an idle claim: a routine on the main account or the board's own run
candidates.statement_a: The coordinator is a routine on the owner's main account, woken by PR events, pushes to main and an hourly schedule, acting as that account.
candidates.quote_a: The coordinator is a routine on your main account, so it acts as that account.
candidates.statement_b: By 2026-10-14 releasing idle claims and overlap notices are a code step inside the board's own GitHub Actions run on the repository token, costing no Claude usage; only epic planning is Claude.
candidates.quote_b: A coordinator step in that same run frees claims idle for 24 hours and tells overlapping work which lands first; Claude splits large requests (epics) into tasks.
candidates.why_it_matters: The release mechanism's trust and cost differ: a routine spends one account's plan and depends on that account's routine caps and schedule, while the board step runs on GITHUB_TOKEN and needs no Claude account; the student onboarding of 2026-10-13 already describes the board's run.

candidates.topic: The board's schedule fallback: hourly or six-hourly
candidates.statement_a: The coordinator runs once an hour, and the hourly run catches a missed event within the hour.
candidates.quote_a: a routine on your main account that wakes on PR events, on every push to main (through a small GitHub Action) and once an hour
candidates.statement_b: On 2026-10-09 the board's cron fallback was cut from hourly to six-hourly to save about 630 billed minutes a month on a private repository; the brief and the taxonomy both say every six hours.
candidates.quote_b: the board's cron fallback cut from hourly to six-hourly, saving a private repository about 630 billed minutes a month
candidates.why_it_matters: The plan's promise that a dropped event is caught within the hour no longer holds; a missed event now waits up to six hours (or longer, see the cron measurement), which changes how soon a claim is released or a board entry appears.

candidates.topic: Whether GitHub's scheduled runs actually fire (the cost and the catch-up arithmetic)
candidates.statement_a: The ladder prices the board fallback as if every cron slot runs: about 750 minutes a month hourly, about 120 six-hourly, a 630-minute saving.
candidates.quote_a: the six-hourly board fallback (about 120 minutes a month, cut from about 750 when it was hourly)
candidates.statement_b: The handoff measured that GitHub ran only 16 of about 87 hourly slots on the test repository's board cron and 8 of about 300 ten-minute slots on the sweep, with gaps of 3.4 to 9 hours, and concludes that every timing claim built on a cron does not hold.
candidates.quote_b: sdlc-template-test board.yml (cron '17 * * * *') 16 scheduled runs from 2026-10-09T09:11Z to 2026-10-13T00:42Z (~87 slots)
candidates.why_it_matters: The 630-minute saving and the plan's within-the-hour catch-up are both overestimates of what a cron delivers; an experiment that relies on the schedule as a timing guarantee, or budgets minutes from it, would be wrong by a factor of about five.

candidates.topic: How GitHub bills Windows runner minutes
candidates.statement_a: Windows minutes count double; a full claude-swap run costs about 72 minutes.
candidates.quote_a: A full claude-swap run (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS and the store zip) costs about 72 of them, because Windows minutes count double and macOS minutes ten times
candidates.statement_b: Windows bills at roughly 1.7x (macOS 10x in both).
candidates.quote_b: Ubuntu runners everywhere; Windows bills at roughly 1.7x, macOS at roughly 10x.
candidates.why_it_matters: The multiplier feeds the 72-minute estimate and any private-repository budget; neither artifact cites the billing page at that sentence, so a planner cannot tell which figure the quota actually uses.

candidates.topic: Which GitHub plan the OpenSpineConsortium organization is on
candidates.statement_a: On 2026-10-08 the organization is treated as Free (or at most Team): the Free-organization quota applies, runs stop when it is spent, and the Free-organization warning about losing branch protection is the one line that applies to the move.
candidates.quote_a: CI minutes now come from the organization's Actions quota: 2,000 a month on a Free organization, 3,000 on Team.
candidates.statement_b: On 2026-10-13 the handoff infers from internal repository visibility that the organization is on Enterprise Cloud, with every rule, review and environment included on private repositories.
candidates.quote_b: Your organization is on Enterprise Cloud, so every rule, review, environment and attestation is included in its private and internal repositories.
candidates.why_it_matters: The plan decides whether private repositories get branch protection, push rulesets, 50,000 minutes and 15,000 API requests an hour, or 2,000 minutes with protection lost on private repositories; the handoff itself marks its reading as inferred, not read from a settings page.

candidates.topic: Whether GitHub Pro and Team's $4 prices are verified
candidates.statement_a: GitHub Pro at $4 (personal account) and Team at $4 a person are given as verified against GitHub's pages on 2026-10-09.
candidates.quote_a: + GitHub Pro, $4 (personal account) | 21 | n/a
candidates.statement_b: The handoff's free-or-paid table, four days later, says the only prices in the docs date from April 2020 and are not confirmed as current.
candidates.quote_b: Pro $4 a month, Team $4 per user a month. Whether those are still current is not confirmed.
candidates.why_it_matters: A cost ladder rests on these two numbers; one artifact calls them verified and the other unconfirmed, so a planner quoting the ladder should know its own repository's later record withdrew the certainty.

candidates.topic: The version of the Claude Swap Cloud PRIVACY.md on 2026-10-08
candidates.statement_a: The privacy statement is version 15, the same bytes in claude-swap-privacy, in the zip and on main, checked 2026-10-08.
candidates.quote_a: The file there is version 15, the same bytes as the PRIVACY.md inside the zip and on main (checked on 2026-10-08).
candidates.statement_b: The primitives spec, also as of 2026-10-08 (main at PR #45), cites PRIVACY.md version 16.
candidates.quote_b: logs and events never carry cookies, tokens, headers, bodies or query strings (CLAUDE.md, Constraints; PRIVACY.md version 16).
candidates.why_it_matters: The store listing's privacy tab must match the published statement byte for byte; if main moved to version 16 after the runbook's check, the zip and the public companion repository would differ from main and the submission text would be a version behind.

candidates.topic: Line count of the Claude Swap Cloud extension and bridge (internal arithmetic)
candidates.statement_a: The table gives the extension and bridge as 14,907 lines.
candidates.quote_a: The extension and its bridge | `extension/src/*` (9,758), `bridge.py` (4,661), `file_dialogs.py` (287) | 14,907
candidates.statement_b: Its own listed parts sum to 14,706 (9,758 + 4,661 + 287), and the 2.2-to-1 ratio is computed from 14,907.
candidates.quote_b: The extension and bridge are 14,907 lines of plumbing around them, 2.2 lines for every line of script
candidates.why_it_matters: The figure is the spec's main argument for Route B and is copied unchanged into the build plan; the discrepancy of about 200 lines does not change the conclusion but shows the count was not recomputed from the parts.

candidates.topic: The cswap size figures (14,907 lines of plumbing, 6,864 lines of script, 19 memory entries, routine caps)
candidates.statement_a: The spec measures the two browser scripts at 6,864 lines, the extension and bridge at 14,907, and reports 19 memory entries read live on 2026-10-08.
candidates.quote_a: The two scripts are 6,864 lines and do all of the reading and writing of a Project. The extension and bridge are 14,907 lines of plumbing around them, 2.2 lines for every line of script
candidates.statement_b: The build plan repeats the same figures as its premise, and the 19-entry export as Phase 1's test fixture, and the routine caps 'from the same plan'.
candidates.quote_b: The extension and bridge are already 14,907 lines of plumbing for 6,864 lines of script, Chrome only, one job at a time
candidates.why_it_matters: The numbers appear measured twice but were measured once; a correction to the spec (its 14,706 sum) would not reach the build plan.

candidates.topic: Routine API-trigger caps, 30 an hour per routine and 100 per account
candidates.statement_a: The plan quotes the routines documentation: API fires capped at 30 an hour per routine and 100 per account, dropped not queued.
candidates.quote_a: API fires are capped at 30 an hour per routine and 100 an hour per account
candidates.statement_b: The build plan restates the cap as runs rather than API fires and attributes it to the plan rather than the docs.
candidates.quote_b: Thirty runs an hour per routine and a hundred an hour per account, from the same plan. A weekly export and a daily board are far under them.
candidates.why_it_matters: The drift from 'API fires' to 'runs' widens the cap's scope; the only source is the plan's link to the routines page, which the spec also restates as '30 fires an hour, an account 100'.

candidates.topic: Branch protection on a private repository needs a paid GitHub plan
candidates.statement_a: Stated as a platform limit, attributed to document 25 and move-gaps.md, neither shown.
candidates.quote_a: Branch protection on a private repository needs a paid GitHub plan. Files over 30 MB stay out of an import (document 25; move-gaps.md).
candidates.statement_b: Stated again, with the admission that it is to be checked on the settings page; the ladder and the store runbook repeat it in their own words, and the handoff later says the organization is on Enterprise Cloud, where it is moot.
candidates.quote_b: Branch protection on a private repository** needs a paid GitHub plan or a public repository. claude-swap is private today; rulesets on the free plan cover part of it.
candidates.why_it_matters: Only the 2026-10-08 plan links GitHub's protected-branches page; the others carry it by hearsay, and whether rulesets on Free cover the protocol's needs was never checked in this cluster.

candidates.topic: A claude.ai Project belongs to one account and cannot be shared
candidates.statement_a: Given as the reason the repository is the shared plane, with no quoted clause or link.
candidates.quote_a: Projects cannot be shared across accounts, which is why the repository is the plane.
candidates.statement_b: Told to the student as fact with no source; the primitives spec attributes it to 'document 25', and only the plan of 2026-10-08 quotes the Claude Code documentation page.
candidates.quote_b: A Project belongs to one account and cannot be shared, so you and [the owner] each have your own; the repository is the one thing you share
candidates.why_it_matters: The whole architecture rests on this one product fact; it is sourced once (the plan, 2026-10-08, Pro and Max beta) and repeated as established everywhere else, so if sharing arrives on Team or Enterprise nothing in the later artifacts would flag it.

candidates.topic: Whether one person's several subscriptions may be pooled for agents
candidates.statement_a: The playbook of 2026-10-03 states that rotating accounts or pooling tokens to widen the usage window is what Anthropic's terms prohibit; such a workload belongs on an API key.
candidates.quote_a: Keep it one account. Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; if the workload needs more than one subscription's window, it is a workload for an API key.
candidates.statement_b: The handoff of 2026-10-13 designs an account pool of the owner's own subscriptions (SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_<NAME> secrets) under a recorded owner decision that acknowledges the terms question, while the plan of 2026-10-08 calls several accounts a grey zone after reported bans.
candidates.quote_b: The owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator of the owner's, each worker on one account's token, knowing the terms question.
candidates.why_it_matters: An experiment that spreads workers over the owner's accounts follows a decision that one artifact says the terms forbid outright and another says is unsettled; the handoff also flags the Usage Policy wording effective 2026-11-12 to re-read before any pooled run.

candidates.topic: Whether a claude.ai/code Project holds exportable knowledge (instructions, memory, files)
candidates.statement_a: The analysis of 2026-10-03 says the Code Project is a work organizer of threads, not a knowledge base, unrelated to Chat Projects.
candidates.quote_a: It is unrelated to Chat Projects: it groups parallel task threads that run in the cloud or, through Remote Control, on your machine. It is a work organizer, not a knowledge base
candidates.statement_b: Five days later the primitives spec exports a Code Project's instructions, 19 memory entries, files, settings and threads through cswap, and the plan treats the Project's instructions and memory as things to carry into the repository.
candidates.quote_b: 19 entries read on the live site on 2026-10-08 (PR #41) ... never confirmed live ... partial: the read is proven, the write is not
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner reading the analysis alone would conclude there is nothing in a Code Project to materialize; the spec's whole inventory is of exactly that content, and the plan's one-way memory flow depends on it.

candidates.topic: Whether the Claude GitHub App is installed on spine-program (2026-10-13)
candidates.statement_a: The onboarding tells the student the Claude GitHub App is already installed on spine-program.
candidates.quote_a: The Claude GitHub App is already installed on it.
candidates.statement_b: The same day's handoff lists installing the Claude GitHub App on spine-program as one of the owner's pending manual steps (issue #72).
candidates.quote_b: spine-program #72 is yours: the Claude GitHub App on the repository, Symphony Setup uninstalled there, each student invited with Write and their worker label made.
candidates.why_it_matters: A student following the onboarding would expect @claude and cloud sessions to work on the repository; if the install was still pending, the Project's first thread would fail to reach the repository through the App.

candidates.topic: Mutants proving the validation harness's checks bite
candidates.statement_a: 59 mutants, each caught, on symphony-protocol main b5f098d (2026-10-14).
candidates.quote_a: 59 deliberately broken copies of the rules (mutants) are each caught, which shows the checks bite
candidates.statement_b: 93 mutants on 2026-10-15.
candidates.quote_b: 93 mutants prove the checks bite
candidates.why_it_matters: The mutant count is the stated evidence that the checks are not vacuous; a planner citing the harness should use the later figure and note that it grew by 34 in a day.

candidates.topic: Size of the coordbench benchmark run

clusters.unsourced_summary: The cluster's load-bearing product facts are mostly sourced once and then repeated as settled. "A Project belongs to one user" is quoted from the Claude Code documentation only in the plan of 2026-10-08 (shared-multi-account-claude-project-plan); the primitives spec attributes it to an unshown "document 25", and the build plan and the student onboarding state it bare. "Branch protection on a private repository needs a paid plan" is linked to GitHub's page in the plan, then carried by the spec (via document 25 and move-gaps.md), the build plan (which says it is to be checked), the ladder and the store runbook, while the handoff later infers the organization is on Enterprise Cloud without reading a settings page. The routine caps (30 fires an hour per routine, 100 per account) rest on the plan's one link and are restated as "runs" by the build plan. The Consumer Terms are paraphrased in the plan, the spec, the build plan and the Slurm playbook with no quoted clause; the playbook's "pooling tokens is what the terms prohibit" and the plan's "grey zone" both lack a citation beyond a third-party ban report the plan itself marks unconfirmed, and the handoff's account-pool decision rests on the owner's word. Both Chrome Web Store runbooks assert Google OAuth lifetimes (refresh tokens from a Testing consent screen die after seven days; an unused client or token after six months), review times ("several days" against "one to three days"), that a lower version is refused, that Public can follow Unlisted without a new review, and that release runs never overlap, none with a page cited. The store runbook's Windows-double and macOS-tenfold multipliers and the ladder's 1.7x and 10x are both uncited at the sentence. The plan asserts without source that GitHub sends no event when main starts to conflict, that a Project with several repositories loads no hooks, and that MEMORY.md's 200 lines or 25 KB is "loaded at start". The brief's Cursor row is written from memory because cursor.com was blocked; its "closest relative is the C compiler experiment" and "most coding work is less parallel than research" are its own judgements. The taxonomy's six uniqueness claims are absence claims from a search that ran out of budget, and its risk 9 (Wayne State AI-tool approval, no BAA on a personal plan, Remote Control unavailable under HIPAA) carries no grade or source. The Slurm playbook's cluster generalities (compute nodes lack egress, home directories read-only, RHEL is what most clusters run, Unix sockets fail on Lustre, --overlap needed from Slurm 20.11, 429/529 retried with backoff) are stated as fact. The handoff names "the enterprise OpenGrid" with no file naming it and infers rather than measures that a routine's pull request is authored under the person's login.
clusters.stale_summary: Everything here is dated 3 to 15 October 2026 and self-labelled as of its day. The analysis and the playbook (2026-10-03) pin Claude Code version gates (v2.1.51, v2.1.183, v2.1.209, v2.1.221, v2.1.234, 2.1.271 pinned in the image), say Glob and Grep are "currently" out of the default tool set, that Code Projects are a public beta on Pro and Max, that retrieval mode's plan availability is unreconciled, and that Anthropic's documentation describes generating a setup token but not revoking one. The plan (2026-10-08) still has Linear as the queue, a routine as coordinator, an hourly schedule, "Pro and Max beta only", an untested bot-wakes-thread question and the unconfirmed February 2026 bans. The primitives spec and the store runbook (2026-10-08) wait on the PyPI publish (publish.yml not yet tagged, tag v0.27.0b1 to push), the first store submission, the memory write "never confirmed live", proactivity and PR-attribution keys "not verified", a never-captured cloud session id, and give PRIVACY.md as version 15 and 16 respectively. The build plan (2026-10-08, sized 2026-10-09) leaves the materializer, the thin Projects and the weekly export routine as phases that no later artifact reports built, and the several-accounts terms question unsettled. The ladder (2026-10-09) names sdlc-template, CLAUDE_WORKER=true, five unchecked setup items, Claude Enterprise pricing unverifiable, and says "the docs flag lags". The handoff and the Beethoven runbook (2026-10-13) list as pending: Beethoven 20.0.0's hand upload (dashboard images still 9.0.0's), beethoven-qa tags v4.0.0 and v5.0.0, submitting Symphony for Chrome and its CWS_ secrets, spine-program #72, deleting five test repositories, "every consumer on 0.4.1 and plugin 0.1.10" not rechecked against GitHub, GitHub Code Security not bought as of 2026-10-08, and the dated changes ahead: pull_request_target blocked on public repositories from 2026-11-02, the Usage Policy wording from 2026-11-12, ubuntu-latest to 26.04 in November 2026, REST API 2022-11-28 supported to about March 2028. The onboarding (2026-10-13) waits on issue 19 (can the grid reach GitHub), on whether the Project offers plugins, and gives CTSpinoPelvic1K v11 and the shared spineps212 path "unless the issue says otherwise". The brief (2026-10-14) and the taxonomy (2026-10-15) say nothing after 0.4.1 is released, eleven fixes sit on main, F8 waits on the owner, the deep lane #21 is unmerged, the canary is not adopted, the push-guard directory bug's fix is pending, the Phase 3 rails (run cap of 10, qa check, public runtime, control panel, account pool) are not built, the coordbench full run of 35 pairs chosen on 2026-10-15 is unreported, the extension is 20.0.0 pre-release, bare mode "will become" the default for claude -p, and the coordination experiment stays out of the grant text until the owner says otherwise.
clusters.notes: Twelve records read whole; the plain text of the plan, the spec, the build plan, the store runbook, the Beethoven runbook, the handoff, the brief, the analysis, the playbook, the ladder, the taxonomy and the onboarding was grepped where a record's quote was not enough. Quotes are copied from the records or the text files as they stand (including the records' own escaping); people are named by role. Two observations not listed as candidates: the taxonomy's "Symphony and Beethoven meet nowhere in code" (2026-10-15) sits beside the onboarding (2026-10-13), where a student's Beethoven session on the grid carries Symphony claims on spine-program, which is use together rather than a code integration, so it is not counted as a contradiction; and the brief's "50 pairs from 20 tasks" against the handoff's "flash 50" subset is left as a wording difference, since the handoff says 42 of those 50 grade.
