candidates.quote_a: On the grid a worker already survives the end of its job: the successor job continues the same Remote Control session for up to seven days, and the workspace stays on the shared disk.
candidates.statement_b: The plan (2026-10-07), reading hpcworker's code at e77863c, says the resume window is 14400 s (4 h), that four hours replaced seven days on purpose after Anthropic's statement, and that the seven-day text in hpcworker's CLAUDE.md and DIAGNOSTICS.md is stale.
candidates.quote_b: It adds `--continue` when `connection.json` is younger than `RESUME_WINDOW_S`, which defaults to 14400 s, 4 h (`framework/lib/profile_sh.sh:117`; template `:302-307`). The four hours replaced seven days on purpose, following Anthropic's statement that a session can be resumed "for about four hours" (`framework/README.md:1087-1088`; `docs/V11_CONTRACT.md:886`). The job's own preempted message also says four hours (`:415`). The seven days at `CLAUDE.md:265` is stale text.
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner who reads only the review would size job windows and queue waits on the assumption that a worker can be resumed after a day or more; the code reading says a successor that starts more than four hours after the last connection.json starts a fresh session. The review's own 'not measured yet' list admits --continue across several job ends is unmeasured, and it repeats the number the earlier plan flagged as stale.

candidates.topic: Whether a claude setup-token (CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN) may be injected into Slurm jobs on the grid
candidates.statement_a: The playbook (2026-10-03) makes a one-year setup token, stored 0600 on scratch and injected as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, the credential for every batch and non-interactive run.
candidates.quote_a: Use two credentials for two jobs. A one-year token from `claude setup-token`, minted on the laptop and stored on scratch, authenticates every batch and non-interactive run: it never needs refreshing, so a job that starts at 03:00 cannot fail on an expired access token.
candidates.statement_b: The roadmap (same day, 2026-10-03) rejects exactly that for Beethoven: injecting a setup-token or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN into jobs is forbidden by the credential rule; the student's own claude auth login is used where it sits. The taxonomy spec (2026-10-15) restates the launcher as 'no API key and no setup-token'.
candidates.quote_b: `setup-token` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` injected into jobs (notes 07, 08, 09): forbidden by the credential rule; the student's `claude auth login` is used where it sits.
candidates.why_it_matters: The two artifacts from the same account on the same day give opposite credential models for the same cluster: a batch job built on the playbook's token-install.sh would break hpcworker's rule that Beethoven never reads, stores or relays a Claude credential, and the hpcworker launcher cannot open Remote Control on a setup token anyway (the playbook itself says Remote Control needs the /login credential).

candidates.topic: Whether several Claude accounts may be pooled or rotated to widen the usage window
candidates.statement_a: The playbook's compliance condition: one account per user, no account rotation, no pooled tokens; rotating accounts or pooling tokens to widen the window is what Anthropic's terms prohibit, and such a workload belongs on an API key.
candidates.quote_a: Keep it one account. Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; if the workload needs more than one subscription's window, it is a workload for an API key.
candidates.statement_b: The handoff (2026-10-13) records the owner's decision that the owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator, designs an account pool of organization secrets picked by code, and describes cswap's failover switching between accounts when a window reaches 90 percent; the review (2026-10-21) then says workers.yml runs on 'the token pool' and the grid starts workers on 'Claude account slot N'.
candidates.quote_b: What the owner already decided. The owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator of the owner's, each worker on one account's token, knowing the terms question. That decision does not change the rule for contributors: no contributor's credential and no pool of contributors' subscriptions.
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner reading the playbook would treat any multi-account pool as out of bounds; one reading the handoff and review would build on the pool. The handoff itself notes Anthropic's Usage Policy change of 2026-11-12 ('services that route requests through consumer subscriptions') and that enforcement could hit every pooled account at once, so the two positions must be reconciled before a benchmark or worker fleet is sized on pooled windows.

candidates.topic: The student's GitHub token for the grid: type, scope and file (onboarding versus the connect-the-grid guide, one day apart)
candidates.statement_a: Onboarding (2026-10-13): a fine-grained token with read access to Contents on spine-program only, saved as one line in $HOME/.beethoven/github_token, mode 600.
candidates.quote_a: Make a fine-grained personal access token on your own GitHub account (Settings, Developer settings, Fine-grained tokens) with read access to Contents on OpenSpineConsortium/spine-program only. In your Beethoven session, save it as one line in $HOME/.beethoven/github\_token with mode 600.
candidates.statement_b: Connect the grid (2026-10-14): one classic token with the repo scope (read and write), 90-day expiry, stored in ~/.beethoven/git-credentials read by git's store helper; a fine-grained token is only the fallback and then needs Contents, Issues and Pull requests at Read and write, with a second token for the student's own repositories.
candidates.quote_b:
One classic token with the `repo` scope covers spine-program and your own repositories at once. [...] chmod 600 ~/.beethoven/git-credentials
git config --global credential.helper "store --file ~/.beethoven/git-credentials"
candidates.why_it_matters: A student following the onboarding page ends with a read-only token in a file git never reads, so the clone-and-push test in the later guide fails with 'Username for https://github.com'; a planner writing a job that reads $HOME/.beethoven/github_token finds nothing after the later guide is followed. The two pages also disagree on whether the token may write (push the claim branch) at all.

candidates.topic: What a Claude session may run on the login node
candidates.statement_a: The playbook's CLAUDE.md allows login-node work up to one CPU core for 60 seconds and 4 GB of memory, plus edit, inspect, submit and monitor.
candidates.quote_a: If it is not set, you are on a login node: edit, inspect, submit and monitor only. Never run anything that uses more than one CPU core for more than 60 seconds, loads a GPU, or exceeds 4 GB of memory on a login node. Submit it with sbatch instead.
candidates.statement_b: The lab recipe (2026-09-27), the onboarding (2026-10-13) and the roadmap (2026-10-03) give a stricter rule for Wayne State: the login node runs only sbatch, squeue, scancel, ls, tail and git; downloads are jobs too; 'Nothing runs on the login node: every computation, render, plot and download is a job, even a one-minute one'; hpcworker allows 'nothing on the login node beyond one sbatch, squeue or scancel per action'.
candidates.quote_b: The login node runs only `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scancel`, `ls`, `tail`, `git`. Downloads are jobs too; compute nodes have internet. | dozens of smoke tests on a node shared by \~95 users (2026-09-21)
candidates.why_it_matters: A worker steered by the playbook's CLAUDE.md would run one-minute tests and downloads on the login node that the lab's incident-backed rule forbids outright; the two rules cannot both be the one baked into a managed-settings image for this grid.

candidates.topic: Whether git works on the grid's login node
candidates.statement_a: The lab recipe lists git among the commands the login node runs, and its session-start routine does `git pull` on the grid.
candidates.quote_a: `ssh -o BatchMode=yes grid hostname` (expect `warrior`); `squeue -u $USER`; `git pull` on the grid; read the top block of `RESUME.md`
candidates.statement_b: Connect the grid (2026-10-14) says git has not been tested on the login node, runs everything on a compute node, and lists 'the command is killed at once' as the login-node symptom; the onboarding's issue 19 asks 'whether git survives on the login node'.
candidates.quote_b: Run these commands in the terminal of your Beethoven session (a compute node), not on the login node, where git has not been tested yet.
candidates.why_it_matters: The SchwingNet pipeline's gate clones and fast-forwards ~/SchwingNet from the login node, so whether git survives there decides whether the gate route works at all; one artifact assumes it does, another treats it as untested with a kill symptom.

candidates.topic: Whether compute nodes have internet egress
candidates.statement_a: The playbook's first 'cluster fact' is that most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly, so jobs must run on a partition with egress or through a proxy.
candidates.quote_a: Two cluster facts shape the design more than any Claude Code setting. First, most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly; Claude Code needs `api.anthropic.com` on every turn, so the job must run on a partition with egress or through the site's HTTPS proxy.
candidates.statement_b: At Wayne State the compute nodes have internet: the student's Beethoven session cloned two public repositories from a compute node (2026-10-14), the lab recipe's rule 1 says 'compute nodes have internet', and the FluoroCap map says the grid's outbound IP is throttled by PMC (so it reaches out).
candidates.quote_b: Your Beethoven session already reaches GitHub: it cloned your two public repositories from the compute node. What it lacks is a login
candidates.why_it_matters: The playbook's site-discover.sh and egress probe are built around a limitation the local grid does not have; a planner importing the playbook's proxy design would add a moving part the lab's own measurements say is unneeded, while its token-on-login-node steps assume the opposite topology.

candidates.topic: Whether harvesters and orchestrators may run on, or fetch from, the grid login node
candidates.statement_a: The access setup (2026-09-14) plans to run the closed-journal refetch from the grid login node because the grid sits in the university's address space, and the FluoroCap map (same day) has 'login-node orchestrators' polling for files and job names.
candidates.quote_a: The grid is inside the university's address space ([the university's network range]) and publishers authenticate by IP. I will run the closed-journal refetch from the grid login node with a browser-impersonating client before asking you for anything.
candidates.statement_b: The lab recipe (2026-09-27), citing the 2026-09-21 incident of smoke tests on a node shared by ~95 users, makes downloads jobs and restricts the login node to sbatch, squeue, scancel, ls, tail and git; the roadmap and hpcworker forbid any polling loop on the login node.
candidates.quote_b: The login node runs only `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scancel`, `ls`, `tail`, `git`. Downloads are jobs too; compute nodes have internet.
candidates.why_it_matters: The FluoroCap pages describe a running design (login-node orchestrators, login-node fetches) that the later rule forbids; a planner copying the FluoroCap synchronisation pattern for SchwingNet would violate the grid rule written two weeks after it.

candidates.topic: Whether the FluoroCap harvesters should use the grid's outbound IP at all
candidates.statement_a: The map (2026-09-14) runs every network route from WSL on the workstation because the grid's outbound IP is captcha-throttled by PMC.
candidates.quote_a: every network route, GitHub and Hugging Face pushes, the sync | | the grid's outbound IP is captcha-throttled by PMC; WSL is not
candidates.statement_b: The access setup (same day) ranks 'try the campus IP first, it costs nothing' and plans the closed-journal refetch from the grid because publishers authenticate by IP.
candidates.quote_b: Try the campus IP first, it costs nothing The grid is inside the university's address space ([the university's network range]) and publishers authenticate by IP.
candidates.why_it_matters: Two pages of the same day give opposite advice on the grid as a network host; a planner choosing where a fetch chain runs (the SchwingNet X-ray and CT fetches are grid jobs) needs to know whether the grid's address is an asset (IP-authenticated access) or a liability (throttled, and a whole institution's range can be blocked).

candidates.topic: Slurm dependency type for chained jobs: afterok versus afterany
candidates.statement_a: The pipeline page (2026-10-21) draws the start word's dependency graph with afterok edges (six of them) beside afterany ones.
candidates.quote_a: One word submits the whole graph with Slurm dependencies. The accented path is version 1, which no longer waits on the multi-day X-ray fetch. [...] afterok [...] afterok [...] afterany [...] afterok
candidates.statement_b: The lab recipe's grid rule 3 (and the roadmap's standing rule) is afterany, never afterok, because a time-limit kill made a whole chain DependencyNeverSatisfied on 2026-09-09.
candidates.quote_b: `--dependency=afterany`, never `afterok`; the child reads a file to decide whether the parent succeeded. | an 8 h limit made a whole chain DependencyNeverSatisfied (2026-09-09)
candidates.why_it_matters: If the SchwingNet chain uses afterok as drawn, a parent that hits its wall time (the X-ray fetch is a 4-day job, the catalog 12 h) leaves every dependent job DependencyNeverSatisfied, the exact failure the lab rule was written to prevent; the planner must check grid/*.sbatch rather than trust either page.

candidates.topic: How long an agent may poll or wait on the Slurm queue inside a session
candidates.statement_a: The lab recipe: no squeue loop beyond about ten minutes; an agent submits, estimates, checkpoints and stops, because polling burned a session limit four times on 2026-09-24.
candidates.quote_a: No `squeue` loop beyond about ten minutes: on 2026-09-24 polling agents burned a session limit four times in one day while the grid did the work.
candidates.statement_b: The playbook's CLAUDE.md: check at most once a minute, and for jobs under 20 minutes submit with sbatch --wait in a background command; its managed settings allow Monitor watches of up to 30 minutes.
candidates.quote_b: check at most once a minute and never in a tight loop. For jobs expected under 20 minutes, submit with `sbatch --wait` in a background Bash command and read the log when it returns.
candidates.why_it_matters: Both are rules handed to Claude; a worker under the playbook's rule can sit on the queue twice as long as the lab's incident-backed cap allows, spending the shared five-hour window the review and spec say several workers already crowd.

candidates.topic: What 'the gate' on the grid accepts: eight verbs, seven words, or the accounts words
candidates.statement_a: The plan (2026-10-07, hpcworker e77863c) says the gate takes one line of at most 200 bytes and only eight verbs: version, status, watch, connect, stop, restrict, read and forget; no verb can carry a prompt.
candidates.quote_a: The gate takes one line of at most 200 bytes in the characters `[A-Za-z0-9._ -]`, and only the eight verbs `version`, `status`, `watch`, `connect`, `stop`, `restrict`, `read` and `forget`
candidates.statement_b: The pipeline page (2026-10-21) says seven gate words (start, status, leaks, v1, latency, fetch <id>, stop) through grid/gate.sh are everything Claude can ask of the grid, returning at most 200 kB; the review (same day) describes words such as `accounts start 1 alpha` with a 60 s floor for start, login and usage and 3 s for the other accounts words.
candidates.quote_b: Claude sends one gate word, and the answer comes back as a file Claude reads. [...] grid/gate.sh one word at a time records every job [...] output, at most 200 kB: branch grid of symphony-template, logs/job-schwingnet-<word>.json
candidates.why_it_matters: Three artifacts use 'the gate' for three vocabularies (the browser-key gate of framework 17, the grid-accounts ssh gate of framework 22, and SchwingNet's gate.sh); a planner scripting a word from one page against the gate of another gets a refusal, and the 200-byte line limit of one is easily confused with the 200 kB output cap of another.

candidates.topic: Gate limits on starting named workers: a hard cap of 3 names per 7 days versus only a 60-second floor
candidates.statement_a: At framework 17 the gate caps every caller at 3 worker names per 7 days, 12 connects per rolling hour and 2 watches at once, per account.
candidates.quote_a: Limits (`browser_key.sh:35-40`): 3 worker names per 7 days; 12 connects per rolling hour, where restricts of a name with no run also count; 2 watches at once. A refusal is `HPCW-GATE limit names|hourly|watch|busy`, exit 123.
candidates.statement_b: The review (framework 22) names only the 60-second floor as the gate's limit and proposes one word that starts COUNT workers (names NAME-1 to NAME-COUNT); the one-per-project plan assumes a worker per project can be started on press; neither mentions a names-per-week cap.
candidates.quote_b: Starting N workers takes about N minutes, because every start waits out the gate's 60 second floor | One word, `accounts start SLOT NAME COUNT`, makes COUNT workers in one call (names NAME-1 to NAME-COUNT), still one floor per call
candidates.why_it_matters: If the names cap survived to framework 22, a project-per-worker fleet or a COUNT start of five would be refused after the third name in a week; if it was dropped, the plan's limit table is stale. Neither later artifact says which.

candidates.topic: Status of the cap of 10 Claude runs a day per repository in Actions
candidates.statement_a: The review (2026-10-21) lists the cap as this system's admission control.
candidates.quote_a: The gate's floor: 60 seconds between start, login and usage calls; at most 10 Claude runs a day per repository in Actions
candidates.statement_b: The spec (2026-10-15) calls it 'the planned cap', among things 'Not built yet', and the handoff (2026-10-13) lists it as a recommendation that blocks Phase 3.
candidates.quote_b: All workers share one person's five-hour and weekly limits; this project's own account reached its weekly limit on 2026-10-15 with several threads running | The planned cap of 10 Claude runs a day; one plan per worker
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner counting on the cap to bound a benchmark's spend needs to know whether it is enforced by a repository variable today or still a plan; the review states it as in force six days after the spec said it was not built, with no build recorded in between.

candidates.topic: How many waiting runs a GitHub concurrency group keeps before cancelling
candidates.statement_a: One running and one waiting run; a newer waiting run replaces the older one.
candidates.quote_a: GitHub keeps at most one waiting run per concurrency group, so a third quick press of Start replaces the second one, which never runs.
candidates.statement_b: The spec's limits table gives a concurrency group 100 pending runs before the rest are cancelled.
candidates.quote_b: | A queue: max concurrency group | 100 pending runs; the rest are cancelled | The board's queue can overflow under a burst of events |
candidates.why_it_matters: The review's rank-1 fix (durable request files) rests on losing a press at the second waiting run; the spec's number would mean bursts of up to 100 are safe. Both cite GitHub's documentation without a line; they may describe two different limits, but a reader of either alone sizes the intake wrong.

candidates.topic: Whether a scheduled workflow can be relied on for periodic checks (the review's 15-minute list)
candidates.statement_a: Rank 4 proposes a scheduled list every 15 minutes to turn silent failures into visible ones.
candidates.quote_a: A scheduled list every 15 minutes (the accounts words' floor is 3 seconds, so it costs nothing); the panel flags a worker whose last word is older than its threshold
candidates.statement_b: The handoff measured GitHub's schedules running hours late and dropping most slots (8 runs in about 300 ten-minute slots), and concludes every timing claim built on a cron does not hold.
candidates.quote_b: Schedules are best effort, and measured here they ran hours late and mostly not at all. Every timing claim built on a cron (the sweep 'within the hour', 'within about ten minutes', 'about half an hour later'; metrics at 03:43 'before the collector's read at 04:17') does not hold.
candidates.why_it_matters: A stale flag keyed to a 15-minute schedule would fire on GitHub's lateness rather than on a worker's silence; the handoff's measurement says the review's fix needs an event trigger or a longer threshold.

candidates.topic: Whether a Claude credential can leave the grid through Beethoven
candidates.statement_a: The review states that no Claude credential leaves the grid and GitHub never holds one.
candidates.quote_a: No port is open on the grid, no Claude credential leaves it, a start by a name that is already running submits nothing, and git is the durable record of who works on what.
candidates.statement_b: The plan found, by reading beethoven-vscode 5.0.0, a path by which an unchecked result id returns the student's Claude credential file to the laptop's Claude (the VS Code edition is a second cluster side beside hpcworker; the fix is 'being fixed separately').
candidates.quote_b: Once any worker has an outbox, the id `../../../claude/.credentials` resolves to `$BEETHOVEN_HOME/claude/.credentials.json`. The relay prints that file on one line, `relay.ts:116-125` parses it as a result, and the tool returns it to the laptop's Claude.
candidates.why_it_matters: The review's statement holds for the hpcworker route it reviews, but a grid that also runs the VS Code edition's scripts (which the owner kept on 2026-10-07) had a read path for the same credential file; a planner relying on 'no credential leaves' should check that the separate fix landed.

candidates.topic: Where node-local scratch goes for a job (SLURM_TMPDIR, /tmp, or /dev/shm)
candidates.statement_a: The playbook stages scratch under $SLURM_TMPDIR if set, else /tmp, and binds TMPDIR from $SLURM_TMPDIR.
candidates.quote_a: Node-local scratch for a running job: `$SLURM_TMPDIR` if set, else `/tmp`. Stage large inputs there, write outputs there, copy final outputs back to `results/` before the job ends.
candidates.statement_b: The roadmap's standing rule is container temp on node-local /tmp/$USER/... and 'never trust $TMPDIR at Wayne State'; the lab recipe adds that /tmp is node-local and swept and puts scratch and IPC under /dev/shm/${USER}_<name>_${SLURM_JOB_ID} with a trap, after sockets of two 18-hour runs were deleted at the same minute.
candidates.quote_b: | Container temp on node-local `/tmp/$USER/...`; never trust `$TMPDIR` at Wayne State | Matches the topic's node-local scratch staging; transcripts and SQLite go there and are copied back at checkpoints. |
candidates.why_it_matters: A job template taken from the playbook on this grid would keep sockets and transcripts where the lab's incident shows the sweeper deletes them mid-run; the three artifacts give three different scratch conventions for the same nodes.

verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 2026-10-03. The playbook is a site-agnostic design for one person's subscription on a shared Slurm cluster. It gives every batch run a setup token, because a headless -p run on the login has been reported not to refresh (issue #50743). The roadmap rejects exactly that for Beethoven: its rule is that Beethoven never reads, stores or relays a Claude credential. Instead it uses the student's own login, and phase 0 measures whether a headless batch run works that way. The scopes differ (a person's own deployment against Beethoven's product rule), but for the same kind of run the two prescribe opposite credentials, and the roadmap names and refuses the playbook's choice.
verdicts.resolution_hint: For Beethoven and hpcworker, carry the roadmap's rule: the student's own claude auth login and no setup token in jobs. Cite the playbook's issue #50743 as the risk phase 0 must measure, and keep the setup token only as a generic, non-Beethoven option.

verdicts.topic: How many waiting runs a GitHub concurrency group keeps before cancelling

The handoff (2026-10-13) explains that such a group keeps up to 100 pending jobs in order, citing github/docs. The review is about grid-accounts.yml's default group, with cancel-in-progress false, which keeps one waiting run. These are two settings with two documented behaviours.

clusters.unsourced_summary: The cluster's operating picture rests on several claims that no artifact measures or cites. The review (2026-10-21) and the handoff (2026-10-13) both reason from a 90-minute limit on a cloud Claude worker without saying where it comes from, while the taxonomy spec's limits table gives a job six hours. Connect-the-grid and the onboarding both warn that the hpcworker framework empties its run folders, with no file or incident cited, while the plan of 2026-10-07 says the new client deletes nothing. The playbook, the taxonomy spec (risk 9) and the plan of 2026-10-07 all build on Remote Control needing a claude.ai subscription sign-in, and the spec adds that Remote Control stores transcripts at Anthropic and is unavailable under a HIPAA configuration, with no grade or source. The review, the one-per-project plan and the plan of 2026-10-07 all describe or depend on a successor job continuing the same Remote Control session with --continue, and all three say it is unmeasured. The review and the spec assert that several workers on one account share the five-hour window and stall together, from the plan's structure rather than a test, the spec's one observation being interactive threads. Single-artifact assertions a planner would also take as given: the review's 'no port is open on the grid', 'GitHub never holds a Claude credential' and 'most hosted agent platforms run on their own vendor's machines'; the one-per-project plan's premise that a claude.ai project reaches a worker only through Work locally and that the environment id is stable per machine id; the playbook's 'most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly' and 'Unix sockets do not work on Lustre or NFS'; the onboarding's 'three refused codes lock you out for fifteen minutes' and 'about two business days' for a grid account; the FluoroCap map's 'the grid's outbound IP is captcha-throttled by PMC' against the access setup's 'publishers authenticate by IP'; the RDP runbook's 'Windows Home cannot host Remote Desktop', 'a sleeping P50 drops off Tailscale' and the P50's CPU generation; and the review's and spec's GitHub concurrency-group behaviour (one waiting run versus 100 pending), each attributed to GitHub's documentation without a line.

The SchwingNet pipeline page (2026-10-21) has the gate words under review in PR #54, zero grid jobs run, one owner press (Connect GitHub Actions after beethoven-extension #23) outstanding, 15 of 20 bank recipes 'to confirm', 22 training entries without a shard, the RSNA RATIC link expiring 2026-10-28 02:38 UTC, VinDr-PCXR access granted 21 Oct, and milestones from 23 Oct to the 30 Oct provisional and 2 Nov talk. Connect-the-grid: write access 'checked 2026-10-14', a 90-day token (lapsing about 2027-01-12), git 'not tested yet' on the login node, and archive links that 'point at nothing' until the owner's script runs. The onboarding (2026-10-13) still routes files through a laptop 'until issue 19 settles', quotes Pro at about US$20 a month and the archive move 'since 2026-10-13'. The playbook and the Chat-versus-Code analysis were checked against Anthropic's documentation on 2026-10-03, with version gates (v2.1.51, v2.1.183, v2.1.208/228, v2.1.233), a pinned 2.1.271 (the image build of 2026-10-07 installs 2.1.283, the action of 2026-10-09 2.1.296), a one-year setup token, no documented revocation, and weekly caps 'introduced in August 2025'; the handoff flags Anthropic's Usage Policy change on 2026-11-12 and pull_request_target's default block on 2026-11-02. The RDP runbook (2026-09-27) hinges on Windows 10 extended support ending 2026-10-13, now past, with Duo ending Windows 10 support the same month. The lab recipe's gap table is 'What is not yet true (2026-09-27)' (167 bare numerals, 0 of 79 manifest keys with a job id, public mirror still v10). The plan of 2026-10-07 is 'Deferred' at 22:33Z, reads hpcworker at framework 17 while saying the live version is not established (resolved as 22 by the review), cites hub SEAMS.md as out of date, and flags the seven-day resume text as stale in three files. The roadmap (2026-10-03) reads framework 11 and extension 12.0.0 with six owner decisions open. The encapsulation report's header still says two pull requests are open while its body says they merged 2026-10-07, and the website renders VS Code terms version 5 against main's 7. The taxonomy spec (2026-10-15) and brief (2026-10-14) have release 0.4.1 as the latest, F8 waiting on the owner, the deep lane #21 unmerged, the 10-runs-a-day cap 'not built', extension 20.0.0 pre-release, beethoven-qa 5.0.0 untagged past v3.0.0, and coordbench's 50-pair run not yet run; the handoff (2026-10-13) says its own claims were not rechecked against GitHub and lists Beethoven 20.0.0 to the store and beethoven-qa tags v4.0.0 and v5.0.0 as pending. The FluoroCap pages (2026-09-14) say a refetch 'is running now', cite a library note of 30 June 2026 on DMC residents' access, and were generated from a repository commit of that day.
clusters.notes: Records read whole for all seventeen members; plain texts consulted for the quotes above (review, one-per-project plan, connect-the-grid, playbook, RDP runbook, pipeline, onboarding, lab recipe, the plan of 2026-10-07, roadmap, encapsulation, spec, handoff, brief, Chat-versus-Code, FluoroCap map and access setup). A sentence-level and 12-word-shingle scan across all seventeen texts found no large verbatim reuse; the duplicate-text candidates are short shared formulations. Names in quotes were replaced by '[the owner]'; the student's GitHub login, which appears in the connect-the-grid text, is not reproduced. Several of the contradictions are between a site-agnostic playbook and the lab's own rules (login-node use, compute-node egress, scratch paths, polling), which an experiment planner would otherwise merge into one rule set; the resume-window, credential-model and account-pooling disagreements are the three most consequential for a worker fleet. The 'gate' ambiguity (browser-key gate of framework 17 with eight verbs; the grid-accounts ssh gate of framework 22 with accounts words; SchwingNet's gate.sh with seven words) is likely three different gates rather than one disagreement, but no artifact says so. Not raised as candidates because they describe different systems rather than one quantity: hpcworker's default worker (2 CPUs, 8G, 8 h, renewal every 8 h), VS Code's (4 CPUs, 16G, 24 h), and the playbook's interactive (4 h, 4 CPUs, 16G) and workspace (8 h) jobs. The clustering gives no superseded or duplicate relations, so canonical_check records how each canonical member stands against the records and proposes one superseded relation (onboarding superseded by connect-the-grid on the student's login). The repository's own memory index (outside the artifact set) states that the template now vendors symphony-protocol 0.5.0 and that Beethoven 21.0.0 exists; those are pointers for re-checking the brief's and spec's release state, not findings from the records.

clusters.cluster: Beethoven: the research engine and its repositories

candidates.topic: How long a Remote Control session can be resumed by a successor job (the resume window)
candidates.statement_a: hpcworker's code tries --continue only when connection.json is younger than 14400 s (4 h), on purpose, after Anthropic's 'about four hours'; the seven days in hpcworker's CLAUDE.md and DIAGNOSTICS.md is stale text.
candidates.quote_a: It adds `--continue` when `connection.json` is younger than `RESUME_WINDOW_S`, which defaults to 14400 s, 4 h ... The seven days at `CLAUDE.md:265` is stale text.

candidates.quote_b: the successor job continues the same Remote Control session for up to seven days, and the workspace stays on the shared disk
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner sizing the chained outer loop (phase 2) or the 30-minute push timer around a seven-day resume would expect a session to survive a weekend between jobs; the code only attempts --continue inside four hours, and whether even that keeps the session is marked unmeasured in both documents.

candidates.quote_b: Metaflow with metaflow-slurm is chosen but not built, and metaflow-slurm is a 0.0.4 release from 2024 that drives sbatch over SSH with a key file, which conflicts with Beethoven's rule never to touch a credential unless its planned plain sbatch adapter replaces it

candidates.why_it_matters: The playbook is site-agnostic, but a planner who adopts its blueprint on the Wayne State grid would allow short single-core work and file polling on the login node that hpcworker's etiquette, the lab recipe's incident rule (~95 users on one node) and the VS Code plan's audit of login-node loops all forbid.

verdicts.quote_a: The login node runs only `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scancel`, `ls`, `tail`, `git`. Downloads are jobs too; compute nodes have internet.
verdicts.quote_b: Run these commands in the terminal of your Beethoven session (a compute node), not on the login node, where git has not been tested yet.
verdicts.explanation: The lab recipe (2026-09-27) permits git on the login node. The connect guide (2026-10-14) says it is untested there, and gives an at-once kill as the login-node symptom. Permission is not a measurement, and no page records git running, or being killed, on the login node.
verdicts.resolution_hint: The login-node half of spine-program issue 19 settles it.

verdicts.topic: Whether the grid can reach GitHub
verdicts.quote_a: Until issue 19 settles whether the grid can reach GitHub, files travel between them through a clone on your own computer.
verdicts.quote_b: Your Beethoven session already reaches GitHub: it cloned your two public repositories from the compute node.
verdicts.explanation: On 2026-10-13 the onboarding holds the question open and routes files through the student's computer. On 2026-10-14 the connect guide reports that a compute node cloned two public repositories, so reachability is settled. It says only a login was missing; the private read with a token is its step 3 test, not yet reported done.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry that compute nodes reach GitHub, from the connect guide (2026-10-14). The private-repository read with the student's token is the remaining check.

verdicts.topic: The file, kind and scope of the student's GitHub token on the grid
verdicts.quote_a: Make a fine-grained personal access token on your own GitHub account (Settings, Developer settings, Fine-grained tokens) with read access to Contents on OpenSpineConsortium/spine-program only.
verdicts.quote_b: One classic token with the `repo` scope covers spine-program and your own repositories at once.
verdicts.explanation: The onboarding (2026-10-13) sets up a read-only fine-grained token in $HOME/.beethoven/github_token as issue 19's probe. The connect guide (2026-10-14) follows it and replaces it: one classic repo token in ~/.beethoven/git-credentials, read by git's store helper, with a fine-grained token at Read and write as the fallback. This lets the student push. In both, the token is typed by the student and never shown to Claude.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the connect guide's token setup. Mention the onboarding's token only as the earlier probe.

verdicts.topic: Whether the shared spine-program archive on the grid is populated
verdicts.quote_a: and the repository holds a link to them in each folder. In a Beethoven session the link opens
verdicts.quote_b: fills once with a script; until he has, those links point at nothing and the files are read from git history
verdicts.explanation: The onboarding (2026-10-13) says the folders live in the shared archive on the grid and that the link opens in a Beethoven session. The connect guide (2026-10-14) says the owner has yet to fill the archive with a script, so the links point at nothing for now. The later page corrects the state; whether the archive has been filled since is not recorded.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the connect guide's state as of 2026-10-14. A look at the shared spine-program archive folder settles whether it has since been filled.

verdicts.topic: Whether Beethoven's trusted-testers Google group still admits students (both artifacts dated 2026-10-13)
verdicts.quote_a: adds it to the testers group and adds your AccessID to the lab volume's access list
verdicts.quote_b: **Visibility Public** (this is the change from 19.0.0), **Trusted testers empty** (the Beethoven-users group served the private listing and is retired)
verdicts.explanation: On the same day, 2026-10-13, the onboarding admits a student through the testers group, and the store page makes 20.0.0's listing public. That page empties the trusted testers and retires the group, leaving the access service's approval check to decide who can use the extension. The store change waits on the owner's hand upload and Google's review, and no page records that they happened.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Once the public listing is live, carry the store page's route: install from the store, admitted by the approval check. The dashboard's record of the 20.0.0 review settles which route held when.

verdicts.topic: How Beethoven is published on the Chrome Web Store (Private with testers, or Public)
verdicts.quote_a: Private, the way Beethoven is published, works as well: it then wants the testers' Google Group address, and only its members can open the listing.
verdicts.quote_b: Distribution set to Public with no trusted testers
verdicts.explanation: On 2026-10-08 Beethoven is published Private, behind a testers' group. On 2026-10-13 the store page has the owner set 20.0.0's Distribution to Public, with no trusted testers. The private state no longer holds once that upload goes through; neither page records the review's outcome.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry Public with no trusted testers from 20.0.0 (store page, 2026-10-13), marked as pending the review's outcome until the dashboard confirms it.

verdicts.topic: One person, one Claude account: whether several of one person's accounts may be signed in and pooled
verdicts.quote_a: Keep it one account. Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit
verdicts.quote_b: `hpcworker accounts start N NAME` starts a worker of its own on Claude account slot N.
verdicts.explanation: The playbook (2026-10-03) holds one account per user, with no rotation, under its reading of the terms; the roadmap and checklist keep 'one person, one account'. The plan of 2026-10-21 runs projects on several Claude account slots of one person: the Wayne State Max account now, and a gmail account to make it two. The positions differ. The handoff records the owner deciding this for their own accounts, knowing the terms question.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the owner's decision of 2026-10-13 on their own accounts, the playbook's reading of the terms beside it, and the re-read of the Usage Policy due before 2026-11-12.

verdicts.topic: Whether several grid workers run at once today
verdicts.quote_a: Since framework 22 the grid runs several named workers at once, each one a Remote Control environment.
verdicts.quote_b: Two or more grid workers running at once on real nodes: no second worker has been started, since that spends allocation and waits on your word and a number.
verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 2026-10-21. The plan states as fact that framework 22 runs several named workers at once. The review, read at 12:03 UTC, lists one worker online and records two at once on real nodes as never tried. The plan's own open questions (shared accounts, resume) show it was not measured either. The design supports it; running it is unrecorded.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the review's wording: framework 22 starts each named worker as its own job, but two at once on real nodes has not been run.

verdicts.topic: Whether a headless claude -p run from a batch job on a student's own sign-in exists on the Wayne State grid
verdicts.quote_a: nothing yet plans research, runs it headless or enforces REFORMS.
verdicts.quote_b: Runs one `claude -p … --output-format stream-json` per request, up to `--concurrency` (default 2), with a 6 h cap.

That edition also allows --dangerously-skip-permissions, which hpcworker's contract refuses. The two statements are about different code.

verdicts.topic: The beethoven-qa version its consumers pin

verdicts.quote_b: Version 5.0.0 on main, untagged (the last tag, v3.0.0, is what both consumers pin)

verdicts.topic: What beethoven-qa's symbolic (CrossHair) check establishes
verdicts.quote_a: no counterexample from the symbolic check (11 minutes 39 seconds on 4 cores)
verdicts.quote_b: Mostly a bounded search: 13 of 165 conditions confirmed over all paths, 152 not confirmed within the bound, on 5.0.0's tree (14 min 3 s on 4 cores)
verdicts.explanation: The two figures are of different trees, qa #4's commit (2.0.0) and 5.0.0, and they measure different things. One finds no counterexample; the other counts conditions confirmed over all paths. Both can hold at once: a bounded search can find no counterexample while confirming only 13 of 165 conditions. The later page does not revise the earlier number; it reads the check more precisely.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the handoff's reading on 5.0.0: a bounded search, 13 of 165 confirmed over all paths. Note that 'no counterexample' is not a proof.

verdicts.topic: The organization's GitHub plan and Actions minute quota

verdicts.quote_a: most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly; Claude Code needs `api.anthropic.com` on every turn, so the job must run on a partition with egress or through the site's HTTPS proxy.

The 2026-10-13 page links Google's Chrome Web Store API page for the setup steps, but neither page cites a source for the lifetimes.

The 2026-10-13 page speaks of a new version of the existing Beethoven item. The figures differ with that scope. Both are unsourced estimates.

So the claim has a source on that page. The checklist repeats it without a source.

verdicts.topic: Anthropic stores Remote Control transcripts on its servers
verdicts.quote_a: Remote Control is unavailable under the HIPAA configuration and stores transcripts on Anthropic's servers

That is a secondary source, not Anthropic's own page, but the claim is not unsourced on these pages. The HIPAA part is the spec's alone, without a source.

verdicts.topic: A cloud (GitHub Actions) Claude worker stops at a 90-minute limit
verdicts.quote_a: A cloud worker stopped at its 90 minute limit keeps only what it pushed
verdicts.quote_b: each six-hourly run or queued issue can start six 90-minute runs

verdicts.topic: REFORMS has 32 items of which 20 are verifiable by code and 12 only declarable
verdicts.quote_a: All 32 REFORMS items can be tied to a gate, but only 20 can be verified by code; the other 12 can only be required as a written field the gate refuses to see empty.
verdicts.quote_b: REFORMS (32 items, 20 as code gates and 12 declared)

It has 32 rows, 1a to 8b, from the REFORMS paper, 12 of them marked Declared (1a, 1b, 1c, 3b, 3c, 3g, 5b, 5f, 6c, 7c, 8a, 8b) and 20 Code. The figure is derived on the page, not unsourced. The spec repeats it, which is one claim, not a second confirmation.

verdicts.quote_a: long runs chain with `afterany`, never `afterok`.
verdicts.quote_b: `--dependency=afterany`, never `afterok`; the child reads a file to decide whether the parent succeeded.

verdicts.topic: Publication tokens live in a mode-0600 file, never on argv or in sbatch --export; publishing waits for the student's press
verdicts.quote_a: a mode-0600 file the job reads, never in `sbatch --export`, logs or the manifest, and never in the extension.
verdicts.quote_b: publication tokens as mode-0600 files, never in argv

Both have the irreversible publish wait for the student's press: the roadmap says 'Drafts prepared automatically; the irreversible publish waits for the student'. It is one rule repeated.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the rule once. The checklist's wording is the fuller one: never in sbatch --export, logs, the manifest or the extension.

canonical_check.why: It is the only audit of the sealed-repository standard across the seven repositories and carries the measured test counts; but its one open decision (VS Code's grid scripts) was taken the same evening in the VS Code plan, and its header predates its own body on the agents and research merges, so the VS Code plan's status line and the pull-request table override it on those two points.

It is the one statement of the six phases and gates; its starting point (framework 11, nothing headless, no gates, two repositories) is dated 2026-10-03 and is superseded in substance by the encapsulation report (seven repositories), the spec (splits.py exists, Metaflow chosen) and the grid review (framework 22), none of which the clustering lists as superseding it.

It is the only item-by-item mapping of REFORMS to gates; its 'none exists yet', 'proposed beethoven-research' and open questions are stale by 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-15, and its same-day sibling, the roadmap, disagrees on whether the mapping was checked against the paper.

It is the release runbook for the Beethoven item; the clustering lists no duplicate though its section 2 (OAuth client, refresh token, five CWS_ secrets, CWS_ON_PUSH) is the same procedure as the store-upload runbook's steps 7 and 8 for the sibling extension, which it says to reuse.

The clustering gives duplicates: []; the two runbooks share the kit, the OAuth Playground steps, the five secrets, the variable and the four-part build number nearly line for line, and the Beethoven runbook tells the owner to reuse the client and refresh token made for the other repository.

The clustering gives superseded: []; on the framework version live on the grid the review (framework 22, measured 2026-10-21) supersedes the VS Code plan's 'not established (10, 13, 15, 16 or 17)' and the roadmap's framework 11, while on the resume window the review repeats the seven days the VS Code plan showed to be stale text, so the supersession runs one way only on the version.
The clustering gives superseded: []; the plan's 'Beethoven (23.x)' of 2026-10-21 supersedes the spec's 'extension 20.0.0, pre-release' of 2026-10-15 and the Chrome runbook's 20.0.0.

clusters.unsourced_summary: The cluster's design rests on a handful of statements that no member measures or cites. The grid's constraints are taken from hpcworker's own CLAUDE.md, not from the node: the roadmap and the REFORMS checklist both say the login node is CentOS 7 with bash 4.2 and Python 3.6, which is the whole reason the gates split three ways and heavy Python goes to the container, and the VS Code plan admits its shell checks ran under bash 5.2.21. The roadmap states that Wayne State is CephFS with a Panasas home with no source, and the lab recipe only implies it (a CephFS volume, pan_quota). The playbook's cluster generalities (most compute nodes have no internet, home is often read-only, Unix sockets fail on Lustre and NFS, the base matches the RHEL family most clusters run) are stated without sources and the first is contradicted by the lab recipe's site rule. On credentials and sessions: that Anthropic stores Remote Control transcripts appears in the taxonomy spec with no grade and in the VS Code plan sourced only to hpcworker's own notice; that a cloud worker stops at 90 minutes is asserted by the grid review and the Symphony handoff with no measurement, and it sizes the ten-runs-a-day cap; that framework 22 runs several named workers at once is read from code in the several-workers plan while the same day's review says no second worker has ever been started; the seven-day resume in the grid review is the figure the VS Code plan showed to be stale text. On REFORMS: the 32/20/12 split is the checklist author's classification of 2026-10-03, which the roadmap of the same day says was not checked against the paper, and the taxonomy spec carries it as a property of beethoven-research. On the store: both runbooks give the seven-day and six-month refresh-token lifetimes, the review durations (one to three days, several days), the 'store refuses a lower version' rule and 'Google does not verify apps with the write scope' with no citation. On GitHub: the store-upload runbook's Free-or-Team quota and the handoff's Enterprise Cloud are each inferred, not read from a settings page. Smaller unsourced shared claims: a DOI cannot be withdrawn (checklist), the framework empties hpcworker's run folders (connect-the-grid), three refused grid codes lock a student out for fifteen minutes and a grid account takes about two business days (onboarding).
clusters.stale_summary: Dated states that have moved by 2026-10-22: the roadmap and the REFORMS checklist (2026-10-03) describe hpcworker at framework 11 and the extension at 12.0.0, two repositories, no gates and no beethoven-research; by 2026-10-07 the encapsulation report seals seven repositories and beethoven-research exists, by 2026-10-15 the spec reports splits.py built and Metaflow chosen, and by 2026-10-21 the grid answers framework 22 and Beethoven is 23.x. The roadmap's six owner decisions and the checklist's three open questions are recorded nowhere as answered except decision 3 (the third repository exists) and, in the spec, decision 2 (Metaflow); phase 0's probe, the headless run and the outer loop are not reported built, while phase 5's store release happened on 2026-10-13. The encapsulation report (2026-10-07) still lists the VS Code decision as open and its header still says two pull requests are open; the VS Code plan's status line of 22:33Z that day records the deferral. The VS Code plan is pinned to beethoven-vscode 631226e and hpcworker e77863c, says the live framework version is not established (10, 13, 15, 16 or 17), carries Claude Code 2.1.283 in the image build, dates the relay and ssh timings to 2026-09-28, and lists a dozen behaviours 'not yet measured' (two Remote Control hosts on one sign-in, --continue across a renewal, a claude -p beside remote-control, GPU jobs, the pilot student's end-to-end check); the grid review of 2026-10-21 still lists --continue across job ends and two workers at once as unmeasured. The Chrome runbook (2026-10-13) says 'upload 20.0.0 now', the dashboard images are 9.0.0's, CWS_ON_PUSH stays unset until then and the release.yml pull request is not yet merged; the handoff of the same day lists the 20.0.0 upload, the beethoven-qa v4.0.0 and v5.0.0 tags and beethoven-vscode #11 and #12 as the owner's pending steps; nothing in the cluster records any of them done, and the extension is at 23.x needing another store release. The store-upload runbook (2026-10-08) describes Beethoven as published Private with a testers' group, retired on 2026-10-13, and waits on a PyPI publisher and tag v0.27.0b1. canonical_check.why: The two records describe the same event: same Saturday, October 24, same Detroit City Fieldhouse, same two contacts, same registration form ([the registration form's link]) and same event page. Several lines are copied word for word. The export's README calls noutom 'the first Celebrate Life flyer'; julcos is the only other one and is fuller (hours, food rule, watch party, the 'everyone plays' rule). Neither flyer says it replaces the other, so the order rests on the README, not on a dated statement. The rewrite also changed the audience (pediatric hematology/oncology to scoliosis and spine conditions), the time (6:45 PM kickoff to 5:00-7:00 PM), the companion event (outdoor Trunk or Treat to indoor Turf or Treat) and the food promise. The julcos record notes it did not read noutom. Superseded is right for the flyer, but the audience change is undocumented, and the old flyer still points at the live form.

clusters.unsourced_summary: Funding page (SchwingNet/osc-outreach-funding-kak2gk): the funder amounts and deadlines are attributed to the funders' own sites by domain only (read in September 2026), and four entries are marked as leads. What has no source at all: OSC's record to cite in every application (802 CT records released, 13 medical students trained, two permanent archives), with no dataset DOI or link given; only the Cureus paper (doi:10.7759/cureus.112661) is cited. Also unsourced: that OSC is not a Registered Student Organization; that the resident cannot apply for 'any student award' (AIDaS ties a narrower version, PI eligibility, to its own call); that a research year 'usually' keeps enrolment; and the $70,000 Community Foundation precedent, credited to 'Wayne State news coverage' with no link. Onboarding (SchwingNet/spine-program-student-onboarding) says the dataset is on Zenodo and Hugging Face as CTSpinoPelvic1K v11, also without a link. Neither artifact lets a reader check the 802 count, and the AIDaS draft's 801 abdominopelvic spines may or may not be the same set. Flyers (SchwingNet/celebrate-life-flyer-noutom and SchwingNet/celebrate-life-scoliosis-night-julcos): every operational promise is the organiser's own statement with no confirming source. That covers the professional coaches from Southeast Michigan (identical text in both), the simultaneous Halloween event (named and staged differently in each), the under-18 eligibility, food provided (first) versus no outside food (second), and the post-event watch party. AIDaS (SchwingNet/aidas-seed-grant-proposal) adds unsourced hardware prices, a $24/h annotation rate and the Joint Commission count; the onboarding adds unsourced student costs (Claude Pro about US$20 a month, paid by the student) and timings.
clusters.stale_summary: Both Celebrate Life flyers are dated only 'Saturday, October 24', with no year. October 24, 2026 is a Saturday, two days after 2026-10-22, so both expire then. The first flyer (noutom, 6:45 PM kickoff, oncology audience) is already replaced by the scoliosis flyer (julcos, 5:00-7:00 PM) but still points at the same live registration form and event page. The funding page (osc-outreach-funding-kak2gk) was written in September 2026, and much of it has moved. RSNA's 2026-27 cycles are 'closed' and open 'next month' (October 2026), so they should be open now. Its pre-October steps (settle RSNA membership and the departmental match) are past due. 'The one thing to do this week' (confirm enrolment, ask Student Affairs about alumni funds) dates from September, and any three-day fast path from a recent abstract acceptance has lapsed. The 2026-27 GME and Senate cycles, and the future deadlines (1 February and 13 March for RSNA and SIR, 16 Feb 2027 for AOA), all need re-checking. The OSC record counts (802 records, 13 students, one 2026 paper) are a September snapshot. The AIDaS proposal's submission deadline of October 16, 2026 has passed, with no record of submission; its faculty PI, department, collaborator agreement and budget lines 1-5 are still 'to confirm', and the manuscript is still 'in preparation'. The student onboarding is dated 2026-10-13, and its laptop-shipping step waits on issue 19.
clusters.notes: I worked only from the five records and three plain texts. People are named by role. Quotes leave out the printed contact names, the venue's street address, e-mails and phone numbers, so some quotes are partial (marked with '...'). Three candidates are internal to the funding page (artifact_a equals artifact_b) because they bear directly on 'in what order'. The dataset-size candidate (802 versus 801 abdominopelvic spines versus the name CTSpinoPelvic1K) is marked as possible, since no record says these are one release. Other things worth knowing that did not make a candidate: (1) The funding page's '13 medical students trained as annotators' and the onboarding's '13 numbered project folders' are different quantities that happen to share a number; the funding record's related_titles links them loosely. (2) The AIDaS seed grant ($20,000, faculty PI required, research rather than outreach, deadline passed) is not among the funding page's twelve sources, and its budget pays for a graduate student annotator rather than the volunteer medical-student annotators the funding page cites. (3) AIDaS says the new DMC fluoroscopy corpus will not be released publicly, so it cannot add to the 'openly released' record that the outreach applications cite. (4) The onboarding has students paying for Claude Pro themselves; the funding page says only the resident-held GME Seed Grant pays for software. (5) The first flyer's HTML holds 2026-07-29 only inside a runtime JavaScript comment; neither flyer prints a year.

numbers_extra.explanation: Both figures are on the same 8,422 held-out crops, but they measure different things. The ladder's 96.7% is the one-vertebra-visible rung of the 48 px annotated-films-only arm. In the reality check, and in the corpus audit it draws on, 'single crop' means 'own validation split, one crop at a time', set against 99.4% for the recurrent head over the run. It does not mean one vertebra in view. The 98.7% row's 99.8% within one and 93.6% NHANES do not fit the one-vertebra rung (99.7%, 84.0%). They come near the ladder's three- and five-vertebra rungs, though they match neither exactly. The skeptic read 'single-crop' as 'one vertebra' and treated two different scopes as one quantity.
numbers_extra.resolution_hint: Carry each figure with its own scope. 96.7% is exact level with one vertebra visible (Level Context Ladder, annotated films only, 48 px, 99.7% within one). 98.7% is the films-only model scored one crop at a time on the same 8,422 crops, against 99.4% for its recurrent run head (FluoroCap Reality Check, FluoroCap Corpus Audit). Neither page names that model's context rung.

review.about: On 2026-10-23 the skeptics' verdicts were themselves read again, the earlier account's verifiers' among them. The sample was drawn by stratum, the 14 clusters and the numbers, and within each by the SHA-1 of the UTF-8 string "stratum|row", rows counted from 0 and the numbers' stratum named Number collisions, lowest first: from every stratum two verdicts that put a candidate on the confirmed list and one that kept a candidate off it, refuted or a number's agreement, then the 5 such dismissals and the 4 cannot-tell verdicts with the lowest hashes left across all strata, 54 in all; and the 4 verdicts whose own quotes the script could not place, 58 in all. work/tools/sample_review.py draws it again from the record as it stood at commit 1c656d4, since the review's rulings and the second reading of ten later moved verdicts between sides. Five re-checkers, three for the verdicts that put a candidate on the list and two for the rest, each told to overturn every verdict in its share, read both sources of each and gave their own verdict, whether the hint was right and the words they rest on. Where a re-checker overturned a verdict or its hint, one of three judges read both readings and the sources and ruled; all 11 rulings sided with the re-checker.
